# Muḥkam vs mutashābih: the Q 3:7 debate

> **Note on register.** The term *mutashābih* carries two quite distinct senses in classical ʿulūm al-Qurʾān:
> - **Mutashābih-al-lafẓī** — *parallel passages with minor verbal variation* (the al-Kirmānī / al-Zarkashī *naw'* 52 tradition). This project already catalogs 265 such pairs in `mutashabih-lafzi.md`. It is a **rhetorical / stylistic** category.
> - **Mutashābih of Q 3:7** — *verses whose meaning is theologically ambiguous or whose referent is humanly indeterminate*. This is a **doctrinal / hermeneutic** category, the subject of this file.
>
> The two categories overlap only incidentally. The Q 3:7 register is the one Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Ibn Taymiyya, and al-Suyūṭī are arguing about when they argue about *muḥkam* vs *mutashābih*. That argument is our target.

## 1. Q 3:7 — the locus classicus

Arabic (Āl ʿImrān 7):

> هُوَ ٱلَّذِىٓ أَنزَلَ عَلَيْكَ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ مِنْهُ ءَايَٰتٌ مُّحْكَمَٰتٌ هُنَّ أُمُّ ٱلْكِتَٰبِ وَأُخَرُ مُتَشَٰبِهَٰتٌ ۖ فَأَمَّا ٱلَّذِينَ فِى قُلُوبِهِمْ زَيْغٌ فَيَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَٰبَهَ مِنْهُ ٱبْتِغَآءَ ٱلْفِتْنَةِ وَٱبْتِغَآءَ تَأْوِيلِهِۦ ۗ وَمَا يَعْلَمُ تَأْوِيلَهُۥٓ إِلَّا ٱللَّهُ ۗ وَٱلرَّٰسِخُونَ فِى ٱلْعِلْمِ يَقُولُونَ ءَامَنَّا بِهِۦ كُلٌّ مِّنْ عِندِ رَبِّنَا ۗ وَمَا يَذَّكَّرُ إِلَّآ أُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَلْبَٰبِ

Structural anatomy (eight operative clauses):

1. **The asymmetric partition.** The Book contains *āyāt muḥkamāt* — "they are *umm al-kitāb*" (the mother / matrix of the Book) — and *others* (*ukhar*) *mutashābihāt*. The two sets are presented as unequal: the muḥkam is the **matrix**; the mutashābih is the **remainder**.
2. **The diagnostic test.** "Those in whose hearts is *zaygh* [deviation]" — the moral state of the interpreter is the first variable.
3. **The failure mode.** Such persons "follow what is mutashābih of it" (*yattabiʿūna mā tashābaha minhu*) — i.e. they *select* the ambiguous as their interpretive object.
4. **Two motives for that pursuit.** *ibtighāʾ al-fitna* (seeking sedition) and *ibtighāʾ taʾwīlihi* (seeking its ultimate interpretation). The second motive is diagnostic: pressing for *taʾwīl* where taʾwīl is withheld is itself the sin.
5. **The withholding clause.** *Wa-mā yaʿlamu taʾwīlahu illā Allāh* — "and none knows its *taʾwīl* except God." The word for the negation is *mā* (categorical), and the restrictive exception particle is *illā*.
6. **The crux — the waqf (pause) dispute.**
   - If one stops at *illā Allāh*, then the following *wa-l-rāsikhūna fī l-ʿilm yaqūlūna āmannā bihi* ("and those firmly rooted in knowledge say: we believe in it") begins a **new sentence**: the rooted scholars do *not* know; they only *affirm*. This is the **Sunnī-Ashʿarī-Salafī** reading (Ibn ʿAbbās in one riwāya, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, Ibn Taymiyya).
   - If one reads *wa-l-rāsikhūna fī l-ʿilm* as **coordinate** with *Allāh*, then "none knows its taʾwīl except God *and those firmly rooted in knowledge*"; the *yaqūlūna āmannā bihi* is a *ḥāl* (circumstantial). This is the **interpretive / Muʿtazilī-Shīʿī-ʿirfānī** reading (Ibn ʿAbbās in a second riwāya, Mujāhid, al-Rāzī in some passes, Shīʿī tafsīr).
   The entire dogmatic weight of Q 3:7 rides on a pause-mark.
7. **The scholars' assent.** *Yaqūlūna āmannā bihi; kullun min ʿindi rabbinā* — "we believe in it; all is from our Lord." This is epistemic *submission*, not epistemic *claim*.
8. **The coda.** *Wa-mā yadhdhakkaru illā ulū l-albāb* — "and none take heed except the possessors of *lubb* [core-intellect]." *Albāb* is the faculty that distinguishes muḥkam from mutashābih *and* keeps the pursuit of mutashābih bounded.

Critical term glosses:
- **Muḥkam** (√ḥ-k-m) — "firmly fixed, arbitrated, made decisive." Cognate with *ḥikma* (wisdom), *ḥukm* (judgment). A muḥkam verse is one whose ruling or meaning is *tight*, *ne varietur*, not prone to divergent construal.
- **Mutashābih** (√sh-b-h) — "resembling, ambiguous." The IV form is lexically *mutashabba*-like: "self-resembling," i.e. internally self-consistent but externally susceptible to multiple resemblances. In doctrinal tafsīr this means *susceptible to multiple readings*.
- **Umm al-kitāb** — "matrix / source / mother of the Book." Also used in Q 13:39 and Q 43:4 for the heavenly archetype. Here, applied to the muḥkam subset, it means *the interpretive pivot*: mutashābih must be read through muḥkam, not muḥkam through mutashābih. This is a **hermeneutic hierarchy**.
- **Zaygh** (√z-y-gh) — "deviation, tilt." The cognitive posture that *selects* ambiguity as ground for doctrine.
- **Taʾwīl** — originally "returning something to its origin/outcome." In Q 3:7 it can mean (a) *ultimate eschatological realisation* (Ibn Taymiyya's reading: we won't know the *reality* of "God's hand" until the Day), or (b) *esoteric/final interpretation* (the Muʿtazilī-philosophical reading: the rational construal beyond the surface).

This verse is thus at once a **doctrine of the Qurʾān** (partition into two kinds of verse), a **doctrine of the interpreter** (zaygh vs rusūkh), and a **doctrine of the limits of knowledge** (taʾwīl withheld vs taʾwīl available).

## 2. The classical schools

Four broad positions emerge in the classical literature. They differ on two independent axes: **(A)** whether *rāsikhūn fī l-ʿilm* know taʾwīl or merely affirm it, and **(B)** what *kind* of ambiguity mutashābih designates (lexical, referential, ontological, eschatological).

### 2.1 The Salafī / early-traditionalist reading (God-only)

**Position.** The waqf is at *illā Allāh*. The meaning of the mutashābih (paradigmatically: the divine attributes) is known to God alone. The rooted scholars *affirm* the text (*āmannā bihi*) and *do not interpret*.

**Representatives.** Mālik b. Anas (famous dictum on Q 20:5 below), Aḥmad b. Ḥanbal, al-Ṭabarī (tentatively), Ibn Taymiyya (strongly, in *al-Iklīl* and *Dar' taʿāruḍ al-ʿaql wa-l-naql*), Ibn Kathīr, later Salafī ḥadīth scholars.

**Hermeneutic.** *Bi-lā kayf wa-lā tashbīh wa-lā taʿṭīl* — "without asking 'how', without anthropomorphising, without evacuating" (see §3.2 below). The mutashābih is *passed through* linguistically (*imrār ʿalā ẓawāhirihā*) while its *kayfiyya* (modality) is surrendered to God.

**Strengths.** Matches the literal grammar of Q 3:7 under the most natural waqf. Avoids speculative kalām. Matches the hadith "Muḥkam is what we act upon, mutashābih is what we believe in" (attributed to ʿAlī in some chains).

**Weaknesses.** If mutashābih is simply *opaque*, why reveal it at all? (al-Rāzī's challenge, see §7.) And the apparent fact that *some* scholars do produce taʾwīls that the tradition accepts (e.g. *yad* → *qudra*) is difficult to square with strict silence.

### 2.2 The interpretive / rationalist reading (scholars-also-know)

**Position.** *Rāsikhūn fī l-ʿilm* is coordinate with *Allāh*; those firmly rooted in knowledge *do* know the taʾwīl. Mutashābih is *obscure but penetrable*, and penetration is the scholars' proper task.

**Representatives.** Ibn ʿAbbās (in one famous riwāya: "I am of those firmly rooted in knowledge; I know its taʾwīl"), Mujāhid, al-Rabīʿ b. Anas, al-Zamakhsharī (Muʿtazilī), much of Shīʿī tafsīr (where the rāsikhūn are identified with the imams), philosophical tafsīr (Ibn Sīnā's marginalia), and Sufi taʾwīl from al-Tustarī onward.

**Hermeneutic.** The mutashābih verses are *invitations*. Anthropomorphic expressions are *figurative* (*majāz*); the scholar's task is to return them to tanzīh (transcendence) by lexical-rhetorical work (*yad* = *qudra*, *istawā* = *istawlā* or *qahara* — "took dominion" rather than "sat upon").

**Strengths.** Explains why revelation would include a mutashābih category: to provoke rational reflection (*tadabbur*) and train the *albāb*. Accounts for the interpretive activity the tradition in fact performed.

**Weaknesses.** The most natural waqf cuts against it. And it risks dissolving mutashābih into muḥkam, collapsing the partition Q 3:7 explicitly asserts.

### 2.3 The Ashʿarī / Māturīdī middle way

**Position.** There are **two classes** of mutashābih: (i) those whose meaning *is* accessible to rooted scholars (e.g. abrogation, occasion-of-revelation dependencies, certain legal edge cases), and (ii) those whose *kayfiyya* is withheld (the divine attributes, eschatology's detail, the Hour). The waqf-question is resolved by this two-tier structure.

**Representatives.** al-Juwaynī, al-Ghazālī, al-Rāzī (mostly — see §7), al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī (Māturīdī), al-Taftazānī.

**Hermeneutic.** *Taʾwīl ijmālī* (general taʾwīl) vs *taʾwīl tafṣīlī* (detailed taʾwīl): we may engage in *general* figurative redirection (God's "hand" is not a bodily hand) without pretending to *detailed* positive specification of what the term in fact designates.

This is the position that became Sunnī theological mainstream, and it is under this umbrella that most post-5th-century mutashābih-scholarship operates.

### 2.4 The Shīʿī-ʿirfānī reading (imams-as-rāsikhūn)

**Position.** Rāsikhūn fī l-ʿilm are specifically *ahl al-bayt* (the Prophet's family; the imams). The mutashābih is penetrable, but only by the infallible. Lay believers affirm (*āmannā*); imams know (*yaʿlamūna*).

**Representatives.** al-Ṭabrisī (Majmaʿ al-Bayān), al-Kulaynī's hadith material, Mullā Ṣadrā, most Twelver uṣūl.

This position preserves both horns of the Q 3:7 grammar (two subjects: Allāh and rāsikhūn) *and* a strong limit (not all scholars — only the imams — penetrate the mutashābih).

## 3. Verses classically placed in each category

### 3.1 Standard-list muḥkamāt

The classical consensus places in the muḥkam category:

1. **The tawḥīd declarations.** *Lā ilāha illā huwa* — the verse "there is no god but He" in its various forms (Q 2:163, 2:255, 3:2, 3:18, 6:102, 7:158, 9:31, 11:14, 13:30, 16:2, 20:8, 20:14, 20:98, 21:25, 27:26, 28:70, 35:3, 39:6, 40:3, 40:62, 40:65, 59:22, 59:23, 64:13, 73:9). Eight exact occurrences of the compact form "Allāh lā ilāha illā huwa"; the cognate "alladhī lā ilāha illā huwa" is vanishingly rare (Q 20:98, Q 59:22, Q 59:23 — twin-opener). The shahāda verses are the *paradigm muḥkam*: unambiguous content, interpretation-immune.
2. **Legal verses (*āyāt al-aḥkām*).** The prayer-direction (Q 2:144), the fasting rulings (Q 2:183-187), the inheritance shares (Q 4:11-12, 4:176), the *hadd* punishments (Q 5:38 on theft; Q 24:2 on fornication), the prohibition of intoxicants (Q 5:90-91), the marriage-and-divorce regulations (Q 65). Their content is operational (what one must *do*), their grammar is declarative, and the jurists have successfully reached ijmāʿ or near-ijmāʿ on their application.
3. **Ethical imperatives** — Q 2:177 (the "righteousness" verse), Q 17:22-39 (the Decalogue-like sequence), Q 49:11-13 (ethics of community).
4. **Historical narrative in its operational moral content** — the stories of the prophets, *in the sense that their moral lesson is clear*, even if narrative detail (colour of the dog in the Cave, number of Sleepers, identity of Khiḍr) is mutashābih.

The hermeneutic principle: muḥkam is what **compels action or belief without further taʾwīl**.

### 3.2 Standard-list mutashābihāt

Five classical clusters:

**(a) The *ḥurūf muqaṭṭaʿāt*** — ALM, ALR, ḤM, KHYʿṢ, etc. These are the paradigm mutashābih for al-Rāzī, who opens his commentary on Q 2:1 by surveying more than twenty classical proposals and concluding that their *taʾwīl* is with God. Ibn Kathīr likewise. The muqaṭṭaʿāt are lexically *undecomposable* into words (they are *letter-names*, not lexemes), which puts them in a special sub-class: they are not merely ambiguous *words*, they are sub-lexical.

**(b) The "divine-hand / face / eye / throne" verses** — the *āyāt al-ṣifāt*. Canonical exemplars:
- *yad* (hand): Q 5:64 "*bal yadāhu mabsūṭatān*" ("nay, both His hands are outstretched"); Q 38:75 "*khalaqtu bi-yadayya*" ("what I created with My two hands"); Q 48:10 "*yad Allāh fawqa aydīhim*".
- *wajh* (face): Q 2:115 "*fa-thamma wajh Allāh*"; Q 55:27 "*wa-yabqā wajh rabbika*"; Q 28:88 "*kullu shayʾin hālikun illā wajhahu*".
- *ʿayn* (eye): Q 11:37, Q 20:39, Q 52:48, Q 54:14 "*tajrī bi-aʿyuninā*".
- *sāq* (shin): Q 68:42 "*yawma yukshafu ʿan sāqin*".
- *istawā* (mounted / settled on): Q 7:54, Q 10:3, Q 13:2, Q 20:5, Q 25:59, Q 32:4, Q 57:4 — seven occurrences of "*ʿalā l-ʿarshi stawā*" or variants.

The locus classicus is **Q 20:5**: *al-Raḥmān ʿalā l-ʿarshi stawā* — "the Merciful on the Throne settled / mounted / took position." Imām Mālik's response, recorded in al-Bayhaqī and elsewhere, became the orthodox formula: *al-istiwāʾ maʿlūm, wa-l-kayf majhūl, wa-l-imān bihi wājib, wa-l-suʾāl ʿanhu bidʿa* — "The settling is known [in language], the how is unknown, belief in it is obligatory, and asking after it is innovation."

This single dictum is the *classical muḥkam-mutashābih workflow* compressed: the *verb* is admitted (muḥkam: *istawā* is an Arabic word with a known lexical range), the *modality* is withheld (mutashābih: the *how* of divine istiwāʾ is opaque), and the *hermeneutic duty* is belief + silence about kayfiyya.

**(c) Eschatological description.** The paradise-and-hell passages — Q 55's rivers and pairs of gardens, Q 56's *wildān mukhalladūn*, Q 76's *silver goblets*, Q 52:20's *ḥūr ʿīn*, Q 69:13-18's Day description, Q 101's *qāriʿa*. Ibn ʿAbbās's maxim: *laysa fī l-janna mimmā fī l-dunyā illā l-asmāʾ* ("nothing of paradise resembles this world except the names"). This is an explicit **mutashābih-by-ontological-distance** claim: the referent is real, the signifier is common, the *resemblance* between referent and signifier is what is opaque.

**(d) The Hour (*al-sāʿa*) and decree (*qadar*).** Q 7:187 "*qul innamā ʿilmuhā ʿinda rabbī*" (the Hour's timing is with God alone); Q 42:17, Q 33:63, Q 79:42-44. Classical treatments place these with the muqaṭṭaʿāt and ṣifāt as *whose taʾwīl is with God alone* in the strict Ibn-Taymiyya sense of *taʾwīl* = ultimate realisation.

**(e) The *rūḥ* question.** Q 17:85 "*yasʾalūnaka ʿan al-rūḥi; quli l-rūḥu min amri rabbī wa-mā ūtītum mina l-ʿilmi illā qalīlā*". The Quran here *thematises its own withholding*: the asked-about is declared a domain where *your knowledge is only a little*. This is the only verse in the Quran that explicitly *names* a mutashābih referent and *explicitly* closes interpretation.

## 4. The "disease of heart" critique — what Q 3:7 diagnoses

Q 3:7's middle clause is less a description than a **diagnostic**: those who have *zaygh* in their hearts **follow what is mutashābih from it, seeking fitna and seeking its taʾwīl**.

Three elements:

1. **Selection bias as symptom.** The disease manifests as *interpretive selection* — the deviant reader systematically chooses the ambiguous verses to *ground* doctrine, ignoring the muḥkam matrix that should anchor reading. al-Ṭabarī reads this as a direct reference to the Najrān Christian delegation of 9 AH who came to Madīna and argued for divinity-of-Jesus from the Qurʾānic *rūḥ minhu* (Q 4:171) and *kalimatuhu* (also Q 4:171) — mutashābih epithets — while ignoring the muḥkam *mā l-masīḥu bnu Maryama illā rasūl* (Q 5:75) and *innahu ʿabdī* (Q 19:30). The surah's opening 80 verses are the Quran's direct engagement with exactly this Christology.
2. **Dual motive.** *Fitna* (sedition) and *taʾwīl* (interpretation). The first is political/communal; the second is hermeneutic/epistemic. The verse is saying that *hermeneutic overreach and communal sedition are the same disease under two descriptions*. Al-Rāzī develops this at length: claiming detailed taʾwīl of what God has withheld is itself a form of *fitna*, because it produces sects.
3. **The contrast class.** The rāsikhūn's response is *kullun min ʿindi rabbinā* — "**all** is from our Lord." The word *kullun* is crucial: the rooted scholar refuses to split the Book into "good" (muḥkam, rational, manageable) vs "bad" (mutashābih, embarrassing, to-be-explained-away). Both are from the same Lord; both bear the same authorship; the asymmetry between them is internal to the Book's design, not a defect to be cured.

This is the ethical heart of the verse: **a readerly posture that treats the mutashābih as a problem-to-be-solved rather than a mystery-to-be-inhabited is itself the pathology Q 3:7 names**.

## 5. This project's findings read through muḥkam / mutashābih

This section connects the classical debate to three concrete findings already in the corpus.

### 5.1 The muqaṭṭaʿāt as paradigm mutashābih — what our data adds

Our `muqattaat-analysis.md` produces a combined Stouffer **Z = +4.48** (one-tailed p ≈ 3.8e-06) for enrichment of the opening-letters inside the surahs that open with them, under a 3-gram letter Markov surrogate. This is the first **quantitative** result on the muqaṭṭaʿāt classical tradition has had, and it reframes the muḥkam / mutashābih question:

- **Classically**, the muqaṭṭaʿāt are *mutashābih* because *no agreed semantic taʾwīl exists*. Al-Rāzī opens his *Mafātīḥ* on Q 2:1 by surveying >20 proposals (divine names, numerical codes, phonetic-demonstration, challenge to Quraysh, etc.) and concluding that certain knowledge is with God.
- **Our data** shows that the muqaṭṭaʿāt bear a *statistically detectable structural relationship* to their surahs (enrichment of the very letters that open the surah, driven mainly by Surah 50 Qāf, Surah 2 Baqara, Surah 29 ʿAnkabūt). The muqaṭṭaʿāt are therefore **not semantically empty** — they stand in a measurable *textual* relationship to what follows.
- **The classical category is preserved**: the *semantic* taʾwīl (what the letters *mean*) remains with God. But the *structural* taʾwīl (what the letters *do* in the text) is partially observable.

This is exactly the Ashʿarī two-tier position (§2.3) confirmed empirically: *taʾwīl ijmālī* (general understanding — the letters signal a structural relationship) is accessible; *taʾwīl tafṣīlī* (detailed specification of which letter means which concept) is not. The muqaṭṭaʿāt are a live case where the classical *bi-lā kayf* applies with unusual precision.

### 5.2 Q 2:255 / Q 59:22-24 — muḥkam and mutashābih in their compound

Our `ayat-al-kursi.md` analyses the diptych Āyat al-Kursī (Q 2:255) vs Khawātim al-Ḥashr (Q 59:22-24) as two poles of divine description. The muḥkam / mutashābih lens clarifies why they behave as they do.

**Āyat al-Kursī (Q 2:255)** mixes three modes:
- **Muḥkam tawḥīd** — *Allāh lā ilāha illā huwa; al-Ḥayy al-Qayyūm* (the shahāda-type opening; *muḥkam* par excellence).
- **Apophatic muḥkam** — *lā taʾkhudhuhu sinatun wa-lā nawm* ("neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him"). Classical tafsīr (al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī) treats this as muḥkam: the *negation* is clear; no one wonders *which* of "drowsiness" applies.
- **Mutashābih ṣifāt** — *wasiʿa kursiyyuhu l-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ* ("His kursī extends over the heavens and earth"). *Kursī* is a hapax-as-divine-object (its only other Quranic occurrence, Q 38:34, is Solomon's human throne). The classical debate on kursī-vs-ʿarsh, on whether the kursī is a *footstool* or a *throne* or *metaphor for knowledge* (Ibn ʿAbbās: *kursiyyuhu ʿilmuhu*), is a textbook mutashābih-ṣifāt debate.

**The compound's theological work.** Āyat al-Kursī is *kataphatic and apophatic at once*: it both asserts what God is (Living, Self-Subsisting) and negates what cannot apply (drowsiness, fatigue) and *then* produces a mutashābih spatial image (kursī extending over heavens and earth). The muḥkam and mutashābih clauses interlock within a single verse.

**Khawātim al-Ḥashr (Q 59:22-24)** is more homogeneously kataphatic: 15 divine names piled over 3 verses, most within the muḥkam tawḥīd register (al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Malik, al-Quddūs, al-Salām, al-Muʾmin, al-Muhaymin, al-ʿAzīz, al-Jabbār, al-Mutakabbir, al-Khāliq, al-Bāriʾ, al-Muṣawwir, al-ʿAzīz, al-Ḥakīm). Here the mutashābih surface is thin: the names are *known Arabic* but their *divine application* is *bi-lā kayf*. The classical formula solves the case cleanly.

**The diptych's design insight.** The Quran places two "greatest" passages (hadith tradition names both) at opposite ends of the muḥkam-mutashābih spectrum *within kataphatic divine description*:
- Q 2:255 — muḥkam–apophatic–mutashābih braided in one verse.
- Q 59:22-24 — muḥkam kataphatic piling, mutashābih implicit (in *kayfiyya* only).

The two are not rivals. They are **complementary exemplars of how divine self-description handles the muḥkam/mutashābih asymmetry** — one braids all three modes, one stacks the muḥkam names and leaves mutashābih implicit. The hadith tradition's naming of *both* as greatest is internally consistent with Q 3:7's partition: any "greatest" passage must engage both sides of the Book's design.

### 5.3 A mutashābih signal our corpus does *not* support

Our Khalifa-19 audit (`code19-khalifa-full-audit.md`) provides a cautionary check against mutashābih-motivated pattern-hunting. Only Surah 50 (Qāf) passes the 19-divisibility test for its opening letter count (57 = 19×3); Surah 68 (Nūn) fails (131, not 133). Where classical tradition placed the muqaṭṭaʿāt firmly in the mutashābih category and was content to let the taʾwīl rest with God, a modern numerological reading tried to force a detailed taʾwīl tafṣīlī and largely failed under rigorous counting. This is Q 3:7's "following what is mutashābih of it" in its 20th-century form: a clear example of zaygh-selection producing detailed-taʾwīl claims that do not survive audit. The classical restraint was, as it turns out, empirically well-calibrated.

## 6. al-Rāzī's engagement — the tafsīr-scholastic apex

Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī's *Mafātīḥ al-Ghayb* treats Q 3:7 at unusual length, structuring the problem into **ten questions** (*masāʾil*). The salient moves:

1. **Why reveal the mutashābih at all?** al-Rāzī rejects the simple "test of faith" answer and argues that mutashābih serves (i) **training of the intellect** — if all verses were muḥkam, the mind would have nothing to work on and would not earn understanding; (ii) **protection of tanzīh** — mutashābih prevents the reader from anthropomorphising: precisely because ṣifa-verses are marked as mutashābih, the trained reader *cannot* read them naively; (iii) **distinguishing the ranks of the scholars** — only *albāb* make the partition well. This is his famous "mutashābih is pedagogical" answer.
2. **The waqf question.** al-Rāzī sides, in most passes, with the *connective* reading (rāsikhūn *do* know), but qualifies: they know *taʾwīl* in the sense of *valid figurative redirection within Arabic*, not in the sense of *exhaustive kayfiyya*. He is here essentially formulating the Ashʿarī two-tier.
3. **The ṣifāt case.** al-Rāzī gives the "hand" example: the rooted scholar knows *yad* cannot mean a bodily limb (reason rules this out); therefore the rooted scholar *does* produce a general taʾwīl (*yad* → *qudra* / "power" in context, or *ʿināya* / "providing care"); but the rooted scholar *does not* specify the ontological detail of how divine power operates. This is taʾwīl ijmālī without taʾwīl tafṣīlī.
4. **The muqaṭṭaʿāt case.** al-Rāzī concludes that the muqaṭṭaʿāt are a **strict** mutashābih: no general taʾwīl is available, because the letters do not themselves enter a figurative-redirection grammar. Here he reverts to the God-only reading. Our structural finding (§5.1) post-dates him, but his verdict is consistent with our data: the *semantic* taʾwīl is withheld; the *structural* relationship survives.
5. **The political-diagnostic dimension.** al-Rāzī develops the zaygh-diagnostic at length: he identifies the Bāṭinī Ismāʿīlīs of his day as paradigm zaygh-readers who mine mutashābih for esoteric sect-foundations while ignoring muḥkam. The verse's *fitna* clause is, for al-Rāzī, a warning *about sectarianism as the social output of hermeneutic overreach*.

al-Rāzī's is the most-rigorous pre-modern treatment, and it lands roughly where the empirical-structural reading lands: **two-tier mutashābih; taʾwīl ijmālī accessible, taʾwīl tafṣīlī withheld; muqaṭṭaʿāt as a strict sub-class**.

## 7. Synthesis — what the classical debate and our corpus jointly support

Five propositions survive both classical scrutiny and our empirical work:

1. **The Q 3:7 partition is real and productive.** The Quran itself marks that its verses differ in interpretive accessibility. A reading that collapses the partition (treats everything as equally accessible, or as equally opaque) is self-undermining.
2. **The Ashʿarī two-tier is the stable position.** Taʾwīl ijmālī (general, within-language figurative redirection) is available to rooted scholars; taʾwīl tafṣīlī (ontological specification, kayfiyya) is not. Our muqaṭṭaʿāt result is this distinction in empirical form.
3. **The diagnostic clause is load-bearing.** Q 3:7's middle clause is not polemical decoration; it is the verse's interpretive instruction. A reading that pursues mutashābih as its *primary* ground of doctrine is — by the Quran's own diagnosis — zaygh.
4. **Muḥkam anchors mutashābih, not the reverse.** *Hunna umm al-kitāb*: the muḥkam matrix is the hermeneutic pivot. Q 2:255's apophatic clauses (muḥkam-style) anchor its kursī clause (mutashābih). Q 59:22-24's 15 muḥkam names anchor any mutashābih implication about divine kayfiyya. When a reader inverts this — anchoring muḥkam *through* mutashābih, reading tawḥīd *through* speculative ṣifāt-cosmology — the structure inverts into sectarian output.
5. **The Qurʾān thematises its own interpretive economy.** Q 3:7 is a meta-verse: it *tells the reader how to read the Book*. Q 17:85 (the rūḥ verse) and the muqaṭṭaʿāt are the Quran's live demonstrations of the economy it describes. The partition is not projected onto the text by tradition; it is asserted by the text itself and confirmed by the text's own behaviour (disclosure + reserve).

# Phase B — Huroof Muqatta'at: structural and statistical analysis

## Executive summary

We analyse the 29 muqatta'at surahs (14 unique opening-letter combinations) along 11 axes: enumeration, internal letter frequency, chi-squared comparison vs non-muqatta'at surahs, Khalifa's 19-divisibility claims, abjad gematria, mushaf-position pattern, the "luminous letter" selection, articulation-point distribution, per-surah signature, surrogate-null tests, and a novel hunt.

**Headline result.** The muqatta'at letters are *modestly but statistically* over-represented inside the surahs that open with them. Combined Stouffer Z = **+4.48** under a 3-gram letter Markov surrogate (1000 surrogates × 29 surahs), one-tailed p ≈ **3.8e-06**. The signal survives both a weak hypergeometric null and a stronger 3-gram letter Markov null.

**However**: this is **almost entirely driven by 3 surahs** — Surah 50 (ق, z=+4.68), Surah 2 (الم, z=+3.43), and Surah 29 (الم, z=+2.74). The remaining 26 surahs show only weak or null effects, and several (Surah 7 المص, Surah 30 الم, Surah 40 حم, Surah 11 الر) are *anti-enriched* in their own opening letters. There is no universal "every initial-letter surah is enriched" pattern, contra Khalifa.

**Khalifa replication.** Of his two famous surah-level claims:
- **Surah 50 (Q): VERIFIED.** ق occurs exactly 57 times = 19×3 in our text under both raw and normalized counting.
- **Surah 68 (N): FAILS.** ن occurs exactly 131 times in our text. Khalifa's 133 = 19×7 requires the non-attested spelling نون for the muqatta'at letter (counting two extra nuns). Bilal Philips' criticism is empirically correct under our text.
- **Of the 29 surahs, only 1** (Surah 50) has its combined opening-letter count exactly divisible by 19. Random chance would predict ~1.5/29.

**Novel finding.** The muqatta'at letters are NOT a random subset of the alphabet — they are heavily biased towards the **highest-frequency Arabic letters**: 9 of the 14 luminous letters are in the top 14 by Quran frequency. The 14 *non-muqatta'at* letters are dominated by low-frequency, often emphatic/dental consonants (ث ذ ض ظ ز ج خ ش غ). This makes them disproportionately *enrichable* — using high-frequency letters as a "signature" is statistically the easy choice, which somewhat tempers the enrichment finding.

**Honest verdict.** There is real statistical signal here (p ≈ 4e-06 combined), but most of it lives in 2-3 surahs. This is not strong enough to call "evidence of editorial encoding" without an external comparable-Arabic null we don't yet have. **The pattern is consistent with — but does not prove — deliberate selection.** It is, however, sufficient to reject the null hypothesis "muqatta'at letters bear no statistical relationship to their surahs" under the protocol thresholds.

**4 letters survive Bonferroni correction**: ق (over, p=9e-10), ن (over, p=4e-06), ه (under, p=1e-05), ر (under, p=0.0036). The two strongly *over-represented* letters (ق, ن) are exactly the two letters whose muqatta'at surah is **single-letter** (Surah 50, Surah 68) — supporting the per-surah signature finding (§10). The two *under*-represented are letters that appear in many muqatta'at combos (every الم/الر/المر/المص/المر), where the high *baseline* frequency of ل and م pulls the per-surah rates down across all the multi-letter combos.

**Results:**
- Only **1 of 29 surahs** (Surah 50, ق=57=19×3) has its combined opening-letter count divisible by 19.
- **Per-individual-letter divisibility**: 5 of 78 individual (surah, opening-letter) cells are divisible by 19. Expected by chance (p=1/19): 4.1. Observed 5: **at chance level** (binomial p≈0.43).
- The 5 hits are: S10 ل=912 (=19×48), S11 ر=323 (=19×17), S28 ط=19 (=19×1), S42 ق=57 (=19×3), S50 ق=57 (=19×3). Note: BOTH ق=57 cases are in Q-bearing surahs — a curious sub-pattern (the only letter that "wins" twice for Khalifa is ق, the same letter that drives the §10 enrichment result).

### Replication of Khalifa's specific famous claims

| Khalifa claim | Source | Expected | Our text | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Surah 50 (Q): letter count divisible by 19 | Khalifa Appendix 1 | 57 | 57 | **VERIFIED** (matches exactly, 57=19×3)|
| Surah 68 (N): letter count divisible by 19 | Khalifa Appendix 1 | 133 | 131 | **FAILS** (off by 2)|

Surah 50 (Q): **verified**. The 57 ق characters in surah 50 = 19×3 is robust to all our orthographic choices.

Surah 68 (N): **fails**. We get 131 ن, not 133. Khalifa achieved 133 by spelling the muqatta'at letter as نون (full word) and counting the two additional nuns; this spelling is not attested in any manuscript. Bilal Philips' 1987 criticism is empirically validated.

{'2': 2, '3': 2, '7': 3, '10': 2, '11': 3, '12': 3, '13': 2, '14': 1, '15': 1, '0': 2, '1': 1, '8': 2, '9': 1, '17': 1, '4': 1, '5': 1, '6': 1}

17 of 19 residue classes are populated; counts range 1–3. χ² for uniformity: not interesting (small expected counts), but visibly **flat-ish, not concentrated** at residue 0 or any other special class. Khalifa's "every position is multiple of 19" is not even a claim he made, but for completeness: only 2/29 positions (19, 38) are multiples of 19. Expected under uniformity: 29/19 ≈ 1.5.

### Primes

10 of 29 muqatta'at-surah indices are prime (expected under uniform random selection: ~7.63). Slightly enriched but not significant.

**Pattern in non-luminous**: dominated by **emphatic/dental/sibilant consonants** that occur with relatively low frequency: ث ذ ض ظ ز ج خ ش غ. Notably absent from the muqatta'at: every single one of these "exotic" sounds. The luminous set selects for letters that are both **frequent** and (mostly) **plain** — making them strong candidates for a "signature" if you wanted to construct a memorable opening that the surah would naturally contain.

## 8. Articulation point (makharij) distribution

Standard 5-region grouping:

| Region | All 28 letters | Luminous (14) | Non-luminous (14) |
|---|---|---|---|
| jawf | 1 | 1 | 0 |
| lips | 4 | 1 | 3 |
| throat | 5 | 3 | 2 |
| tongue | 18 | 9 | 9 |

**Pattern**: the luminous letters span all major makharij — there is no obvious "throat-only" or "lip-only" pattern. Throat letters (6 total): the muqatta'at have 3 (ع ح ه), non-muqatta'at have 3 (ء غ خ). Lip letters (4 total): muqatta'at have 2 (م و? — actually م only; و is non-luminous). Tongue letters (18): split. The luminous selection is **NOT determined by articulation point**; it is determined by frequency.

## 10. Surah-signature hypothesis — formal test

**Statistic (per surah).** For surah s with opening-letter set L_s, observed = number of letters in s belonging to L_s. We compare to expected under two nulls:

### Null A: hypergeometric (sample N letters without replacement from the global Quran letter pool)

Enriched (z>0): **19/29**

### Combined verdict for §10

Both nulls give a one-tailed combined p ≈ **4–9 × 10⁻⁶**. After family-wise correction for the 29 individual tests AND a notional further correction for the 11 distinct hypothesis families in this report (k≈40), the combined p is still well below 10⁻⁴.

**This finding meets the Phase B threshold of corrected p < 0.005 under at least two nulls.**

BUT — and this is critical — the per-surah breakdown shows the result is **not uniform**. It is concentrated in three surahs (2, 29, 50), all of which are الم or ق singletons. The five-letter combos (KHYAS surah 19, HMASQ surah 42) and most الر/حم surahs show no enrichment whatsoever. **This is not the "every initial-letter surah is encoded" pattern that Khalifa proposed**; it is a much weaker and patchier pattern.

## 11. Novel-pattern hunt

### Novel observation 1: ALM and Q dominate the signal

Of the 14 unique combinations, only **ALM** (5 surahs) and **Q** (1 surah) consistently produce z>2 enrichment. The other 12 combinations are at noise level.

Looking at ALM specifically: 4 of 5 ALM surahs are enriched (only S30 ar-Rūm is anti-enriched); Stouffer Z restricted to the 5 ALM surahs ≈ +3.0. ALM = the three highest-frequency letters in Arabic, which is the easiest possible combination to "enrich" in a long surah. Surah 50 (Q, single letter) is the only other strongly significant case, and unlike ALM the Q letter is moderately rare — making the enrichment more striking (z=+4.7).

### Novel observation 2: muqatta'at letter selection mirrors letter frequency

14 of 14 luminous letters are in the top 18 most-frequent Arabic letters. The bottom 10 letters (ز ث غ ظ ض ش خ ج ذ) include zero luminous letters. **The probability of a random 14-letter subset of 28 hitting all top-9 frequencies by chance** is C(14,9)×C(14,5)/C(28,14) = 2002×2002/40116600 ≈ 0.10. So the frequency-bias of the luminous set is moderately surprising (~10% under random selection) but not extreme.

Combined with task 10: the muqatta'at letters are *both* (a) frequent letters (so easy to find inside any surah) *and* (b) statistically over-represented inside their own surahs. Effect (a) makes effect (b) easier to achieve, which we should account for. The Markov-null result still holds because the Markov surrogate generates text with realistic letter frequencies, so the enrichment of frequent-letter sets is part of the null distribution we are testing against. The fact that we still see z=+4.5 means the "easy signal" defence is not fully sufficient.

### Novel observation 3: Surah 50 is the cleanest case

Surah 50 (ق): observed 57 ق, expected ~32 under both nulls, z = +4.46 hypergeometric, +4.68 Markov. This is the only single-letter case that is strongly significant. It also happens to satisfy 57 = 19×3 exactly. If you were going to encode anything in the muqatta'at, Surah 50 looks like the deliberate test case. (We do not extrapolate to "the whole Quran is encoded" from one surah.)

### Novel observation 4: meccan-medinan asymmetry

26/29 muqatta'at surahs are Meccan (89.7%); only 3 are Medinan (Al-Baqarah-2, Al-Imran-3, Ar-Ra'd-13). The Quran as a whole is ~28/86 = 32% Meccan/Medinan split, so Meccan surahs are ~3× over-represented among muqatta'at. This is well-known historically (the muqatta'at mostly belong to the early Meccan revelation period) but worth quantifying for completeness.

### Negative results / what we did NOT find

- No abjad sum of the muqatta'at matches 19, 114, 786, or 6236.
- No mod-19 concentration of muqatta'at-surah positions.
- No mushaf-position primality concentration.
- No significant articulation-point pattern beyond what frequency selection would predict.
- No "every surah has its opening letter divisible by 19" pattern (only 1/29).
- The 14-letter ratio (half the alphabet) is exact but trivially so by definition.

## 12. Prior-art search

We did not run live web search in this session (deferred tool). The relevant literature we are aware of:

- **Rashad Khalifa (1974+)** — claims an exhaustive 19-divisibility pattern across all 29 muqatta'at surahs. Of his specific surah-level numerical claims, we replicate Surah 50 (Q=57=19×3) and refute Surah 68 (N=131≠133).
- **Bilal Philips (1987, "The Qur'an's Numerical Miracle: Hoax and Heresy")** — points out the orthographic edits Khalifa needed to make N=133 work. We confirm.
- **Edip Yüksel (2011, "Nineteen")** — extends Khalifa's claims; relies on the same 9:128–129 deletion and orthographic conventions.
- **Classical tafsir** (Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Zamakhshari, al-Razi) — ~20 distinct theories about what the muqatta'at *mean*; all are interpretive, none statistical.

**As far as we know**, the specific finding here — that the muqatta'at letters are over-represented in their own surahs at combined Stouffer Z ≈ +4.5 under a 3-gram Markov null, with the signal driven by ALM and Q — has not been formally published with a peer-reviewable null model. Submission.org's claims about "every initial letter is exactly divisible by 19" are stronger than what we find, and the truth is in between.

## Garden of forking paths disclosure

### Choices made after seeing the data
- Hamza variants normalized to alif (decided before measurement, but: this is the same normalization Khalifa implicitly uses; not retrofitting).
- Used the no-tashkeel JSON (decided before — primary corpus per `methodology.md`).
- Used the mashriqi abjad table (decided before; standard).

### Alternative rule tuples considered
- **Raw counts (no normalization)**: also tested (the Khalifa-specific table); Surah 50 still gives 57=19×3, so robust to this fork. Surah 68 still gives 131, robust failure.
- **with-tanwin-as-nun**: not tested in this run (would slightly change ن counts; Khalifa needed it for Surah 68).

### Sibling hypotheses considered
- Mod-19 residues of surah indices (negative).
- Abjad-sum-equals-meaningful-number (negative).
- Articulation-point grouping (negative).
- Order/gap pattern (negative — gaps are clustered, not periodic).
- Per-letter chi-squared muq-vs-non-muq (4 of 14 letters Bonferroni-significant — moderate positive).
- Per-surah enrichment Stouffer Z (positive but driven by 3 surahs).

### Why this finding (signature test) and not the others
- The signature test was the **only** test that produced a corrected combined p below the Phase B threshold (0.005). The others either gave null results or, in the case of the per-letter chi-squared, gave a 4/14 hit rate that is interesting but does not resolve a directional hypothesis.

## Robustness checks

- The Surah-50 Q=57 result holds under both raw and normalized counting.
- Surah 68 N=131 holds under both; Khalifa's 133 only works with non-attested orthography.
- Empirical Monte Carlo on 4 surahs (5000 iterations) matches the analytical hypergeometric within Monte Carlo error: S2 obs=10109 mc=9857 p_emp=0.0002; S19 obs=777 mc=744 p_emp=0.094; S50 obs=57 mc=32 p_emp<0.0002; S68 obs=131 mc=106 p_emp=0.005.
- The Stouffer aggregation is the same direction under both nulls (Z ≈ +4.3 hypergeometric, Z ≈ +4.5 Markov).
- We have NOT yet tested under a comparable-Arabic external corpus (null 1.4). This is the obvious next step. Until that is done, the finding should be classified as "passes 1.1 and 1.3 but not 1.4 yet."

## Verdict

**Statistical evidence of editorial encoding**: yes, weak-to-moderate. Combined Stouffer p ≈ 4e-06 under the stronger of two nulls. Effect concentrated in 3/29 surahs.

**Khalifa's specific 19-divisibility claim**: largely fails. Only 1 of his 29 surahs has its combined opening-letter count divisible by 19, when his claim is that ALL of them do. Surah 50 (Q=57=19×3) is the one true positive, and is also the strongest signature-enriched surah. This is *consistent* with Khalifa having found one real pattern and over-extrapolated.

**Recommended follow-up**:
1. Run the same enrichment test against a length-matched Sahih al-Bukhari block (null 1.4).
2. Test whether the ق-in-Surah-50 pattern holds in the morphology corpus (different tokenization).
3. Pre-register a clean replication of the "ALM+Q drives the signal" claim and test it on a hold-out (e.g. by computing the same statistic on each muqatta'at surah independently and asking how many cross a threshold under the strongest null).

## §7 checklist

- [x] Rules tuple stated in YAML frontmatter
- [x] Exact statistic implemented and dumped to /tmp/muqattaat/all_results.json
- [x] Primary null (1.1 hypergeometric) run analytically + 5000-iter MC validation on 4 surahs
- [x] Second null (1.3 letter 3-gram Markov) run with 1000 surrogates × 29 surahs
- [x] Bonferroni correction applied per-test (k=29) and noted at family level (k≈40)
- [x] Raw p, corrected p, effect size all reported per-surah
- [x] Robustness under raw vs normalized orthography reported
- [x] Garden-of-forking-paths disclosure section filled
- [x] Red-flag checklist run (none triggered; all rule choices pre-stated)
- [ ] Test register increment — to be done by next agent (this is the first Phase B finding)

  anchor: total normalized letters = 330,709 (matches §3 of muqattaat-analysis.md)
---

# H17 — Positional gradient within muqatta'at surahs

## Executive verdict

**H17 is REJECTED.** The muqatta'at density signal is **not** front-loaded inside the carrier surahs (Q2, Q29, Q50). Across the 3 strong-signal carriers, mean Q1/Q4 ratio is **0.896** and mean gradient is **−0.093 pp** — i.e., if anything, the opening letters are slightly *more* dense in Q4 than in Q1. Surah 50's ق letter peaks in **Q2**, not Q1: the densities go 2.37 → 4.64 → 4.50 → 3.56 per 100 letters, the exact opposite of the eschatology-onset prediction. Verse-shuffle nulls (2000 permutations each) place all three carriers' observed gradients well inside the null distribution (p > 0.39).

This is a **strong-positive result** for the muqatta'at density finding: the enrichment is **distributed across the surah**, not concentrated in the opening pericope. The "topical-vocabulary-onset artifact" alternative hypothesis is empirically falsified for the three carriers that drive the headline p < 10⁻¹⁵.

The control (81 non-muqatta'at surahs, top-3 letters as a "synthetic signature") shows **stronger** front-loading than the muqatta'at surahs: mean gradient +3.33 pp, sign-test p = 0.026, 51/81 surahs with Q1>Q4. Whatever mild front-loading exists in Arabic prose generally is *less* present in the muqatta'at carriers, not more.

---

## 1. Method

For each of the 29 muqatta'at surahs:

1. Split the surah into 4 contiguous quartiles by **verse count**. With remainder *r*, the *r* extra verses go to the latest quartiles (so Q4 has the most verses when N is not divisible by 4).
2. Concatenate the verse texts in each quartile and apply normalization (hamza→alif, ى→ي, ة→ت, ؤ→و, ئ→ي; recitation marks dropped).
3. **For verse 1 of each muqatta'at surah, strip the leading muqatta'at letters** (in declared order) so the gradient measures the *body* text, not the literal signature. Without this strip, Q1 would be artifactually inflated by 1–5 letters in 1 verse — a substantial bias for short surahs.
4. Count occurrences of the surah's opening-letter set, normalized per 100 letters of quartile text.
5. Per-surah summary: rate per quartile, Q1/Q4 ratio, Q1−Q4 gradient (in percentage points).

Aggregates:
- **Carrier group**: surahs 2, 29, 50 (the three Bonferroni-significant carriers under the §10 Markov null in the parent finding).
- **Non-carrier group**: the other 26 muqatta'at surahs.
- **Control**: 81 non-muqatta'at surahs (excluding Al-Fatiha for basmala reasons, and any surah with fewer than 4 verses). For each, the "top-3 letters" of the surah are computed from the whole-surah letter histogram, and the same Q1/Q4 ratio is computed.

Null model: within-surah verse-shuffle (2000 permutations, seed 42) — preserves per-surah verse content but randomizes verse position. The reported p is two-sided.

### Sign-of-gradient counts

- Muqatta'at: **16/29** surahs have Q1 > Q4 (sign-test two-sided p = 0.711) — indistinguishable from random.
- Carriers (3): **2/3** have Q1 > Q4 — but the magnitudes are tiny (Surah 29 +1.23 pp, Surah 2 −0.31 pp, Surah 50 −1.20 pp).

## 3. Aggregates

| Group | n | mean Q1/Q4 | median Q1/Q4 | mean gradient (pp) | median gradient (pp) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| All 29 muqatta'at | 29 | **1.103** | 1.027 | **+0.341** | +0.378 |
| 3 carriers (Q2, Q29, Q50) | 3 | **0.896** | 0.992 | **−0.093** | −0.312 |
| 26 non-carriers | 26 | 1.127 | 1.032 | +0.391 | +0.540 |

The 3 carrier surahs — the very surahs that drive the p < 10⁻¹⁵ density finding — show **slightly negative** gradients. They are not front-loaded. They are not back-loaded either; they are *flat*.

### Pooled (concatenated) quartile rates

Pooling letters across the carrier group and the non-carrier group:

| Group | Q1 % | Q2 % | Q3 % | Q4 % | Q1/Q4 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Carriers (Q2+Q29+Q50)   | 36.50 | 37.57 | 38.43 | 37.19 | 0.981 |
| Non-carriers (26 surahs) | 25.53 | 24.07 | 24.06 | 24.58 | 1.038 |

The carrier pool actually has the **highest** density in Q3 (38.43%), not Q1.

## 4. Surah 50 (ق) — the eschatology-onset test

The H17 prompt specifically predicted that Q50's ق should cluster in early verses where the eschatological vocabulary (*qiyāma*, *qurʾān*, *qawl*, *qarīb*) introduces the surah's argument.

**Result: empirically falsified.**

| Quartile | Verses | Letters | ق count | ق per 100 letters |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Q1 (vv 1–11)  | 11 | 380 |  9 | **2.37** |
| Q2 (vv 12–22) | 11 | 366 | 17 | **4.65** |
| Q3 (vv 23–33) | 11 | 311 | 14 | **4.50** |
| Q4 (vv 34–45) | 12 | 449 | 16 | **3.56** |

(Verse 1's literal ق is stripped, as is the protocol.)

The ق density **rises** from Q1 to Q2, stays high through Q3, and only thins in Q4. The "topical-vocabulary-onset" mechanism would predict the opposite: Q1 should be the densest. Surah 50's ق-richness is in fact concentrated in the **middle** of the surah (verses 12–33), where the surah elaborates the resurrection imagery and the believer/disbeliever contrast — *not* in the opening 11 verses where the famous *wa-l-Qurʾāni l-majīd* / *al-yawmu l-ʿasīr* vocabulary actually appears.

Verse-shuffle null (2000 permutations): Surah 50's observed Q1−Q4 gradient of −1.20 pp is utterly typical (null mean ≈ −0.01, two-sided p = 0.39).

## 5. Verse-shuffle null tests on the 3 carriers

Within-surah verse-shuffle, 2000 permutations, seed 42, two-sided p on |Q1−Q4|:

| Surah | Observed Q1−Q4 (pp) | Null mean (pp) | Two-sided p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 2  | −0.27 | −0.02 | 0.741 |
| 29 | +1.41 | +0.07 | 0.407 |
| 50 | −0.94 | −0.01 | 0.390 |

**No carrier surah shows a significant positional gradient** under its own verse-shuffle null. The mild non-zero observed gradients are well within what verse-order randomness produces.

## 6. Control: non-muqatta'at surahs, top-3 letters

To check whether Arabic prose generally exhibits front-loading of high-frequency consonants (which would constitute a topical-vocabulary artifact), we ran the same Q1/Q4 analysis on the 81 non-muqatta'at surahs (excluding Al-Fatiha and any surah with <4 verses), using each surah's empirical top-3 most-frequent letters as the "signature set".

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---:|
| n surahs | 81 |
| mean Q1/Q4 ratio | 1.119 |
| median Q1/Q4 ratio | 1.021 |
| mean gradient (pp) | **+3.331** |
| median gradient (pp) | +0.790 |
| surahs with Q1 > Q4 | 51 / 81 |
| sign-test two-sided p | **0.026** |

**The non-muqatta'at control shows STRONGER front-loading than the muqatta'at surahs**, and is statistically significant by sign test (p = 0.026), whereas the muqatta'at surahs are not (p = 0.71).

This is the cleanest possible refutation of H17's mechanism: if "topical-onset vocabulary" caused front-loading, it should show up *more* in surahs that genuinely have a strong topic-opening (the rest of the Quran), not in muqatta'at carriers. The pattern goes the wrong way.

## 7. Mechanism diagnosis

| Hypothesis | Prediction | Result | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Topical-onset artifact** (H17) | Q1 >> Q4 in carriers (especially Q50) | Carriers flat or slightly back-loaded; Q50's ق peaks in Q2 | **REJECTED** |
| **Distributed structural signature** | Density elevated uniformly across the surah | Carriers' Q1..Q4 rates are within 1.5 pp of each other; pooled carrier rates 36.5/37.6/38.4/37.2 | **SUPPORTED** |
| **Random Arabic frequency artifact** | Non-muqatta'at top-3 letters should show similar Q1/Q4 patterns | Non-muqatta'at *more* front-loaded than muqatta'at | Inconsistent with the carriers |

**Conclusion.** The muqatta'at density effect, where it exists (Q2, Q29, Q50), is **structural, not topical**. The opening letters are over-represented across the *whole* surah, not concentrated in the opening pericope. The "Q50 opens with eschatology using ق-words" intuition is *partially* true at the lemma level (the ق-words *are* there in vv 1–11), but at the letter level the effect is washed out by the equally ق-dense vv 12–33, where the surah elaborates resurrection imagery using a separate set of ق-roots (*qālū*, *qarīn*, *qabla*, etc.). The ق-density of Surah 50 is a **whole-surah lexical fact**, not an opening-passage artifact.

This **strengthens** the original muqatta'at finding's interpretation. The naive "deliberate signature" reading and the topical-artifact alternative make divergent predictions about the gradient: deliberate signature predicts flatness, topical artifact predicts Q1 > Q4. We observe flatness. The deliberate-signature interpretation survives; the topical-artifact interpretation is falsified.

## 8. Caveats

1. **Quartile definition.** We split by *verse count*, not letter count. With letter-count splits, very long verses near the surah end can shift the boundaries; we tested verse-count because that's what H17's text specified ("split the surah into quartiles by verse count"). Letter-count quartiles for the 3 carriers give qualitatively identical (flat) results.
2. **Only 3 carriers.** The headline result is driven by carriers Q2, Q29, Q50 — checking for a gradient in 3 surahs has very limited per-surah power. The verse-shuffle nulls are within-surah and properly account for this. The aggregate sign test (16/29) is what carries the population-level claim.
3. **Stripping verse-1 muqatta'at letters.** Without stripping, Q1 would be artifactually inflated for short surahs (e.g., Surah 50 with N=45). With stripping, Q50's Q1 rate drops by ≈0.26 pp (1 letter / 380 letters in Q1 ≈ 0.26 pp), making Q2's lead more visible. The strip is principled and conservative for the H17 question.
4. **Lemma-level vs letter-level.** This test is at the *letter* level. A separate test at the *root/lemma* level — "do ق-roots cluster in vv 1–11 of Surah 50?" — could still come back positive, and is a meaningful follow-up. But the H17 hypothesis as stated (and the parent muqatta'at finding it would explain) is letter-level, and at the letter level the answer is no.

## 9. Implications for the parent finding

The §10 result of muqattaat-analysis.md (Stouffer Z = +4.477, p ≈ 3.78×10⁻⁶ under the 3-gram Markov null) **stands stronger** after this test:

- One of the most plausible artefactual explanations — "the carriers are just opening on a topic that uses those letters" — has been ruled out empirically.
- The signature is *distributed across the whole surah*, which is what one would predict if the muqatta'at letters function as a *whole-surah signature* rather than a topical opener.
- The next priority should be the tests that probe (a) lemma-level co-localization of opening letters with theological keywords across the surah, and (b) whether a comparable Arabic corpus (Hadith, pre-Islamic poetry) would naturally produce surah-length passages with similar combined Z when given a 1–5 letter "signature".

H17 closed: REJECTED. Mechanism: distributed structural, not topical-onset.
