# Sacrifice and Vow Theology in the Qurʾān

**Phase B hypothesis document.** Data source: `data/morphology/quranic-corpus-morphology-0.4.txt`. All verse references verified against the Quranic Arabic Corpus morphology. Roman transliteration uses the Buckwalter scheme in queries; a reader-friendly transliteration is given in the body.

---

## 1. Per-Word Inventory

### 1.1 Root `*bH` — dhabaḥa "to slaughter (ritually)"

Nine occurrences in three distinct pragmatic fields.

| Ref | Form | Vocalized | Gloss | Speaker/context |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2:49 | `yu*ab~iHu` | yudhabbiḥu (Form II) | "slaughters (intensively)" | Pharaoh slaughtering Israelite sons |
| 2:67 | `ta*obaHu` | tadhbaḥū | "you slaughter (cow)" | Moses to his people |
| 2:71 | `*abaHu` | dhabaḥū | "they slaughtered" | Moses' people finally obey |
| 5:3 | `*ubiHa` | dhubiḥa (PASS) | "was slaughtered" | prohibition of altar-sacrifices |
| 14:6 | `yu*ab~iHu` | yudhabbiḥu | "slaughters" | Pharaoh's oppression recalled |
| 27:21 | `>a*obaHa` | adhbaḥannahu | "I shall surely slaughter him" | Solomon threatens hoopoe |
| 28:4 | `yu*ab~iHu` | yudhabbiḥu | "slaughters" | Pharaoh again |
| 37:102 | `>a*obaHu` | adhbaḥu-ka | "I slaughter you" | Abraham to Ishmael |
| 37:107 | `*iboHK` | dhibḥin (noun) | "a slaughter-offering" | ransom for Ishmael |

Form II `yudhabbiḥu` (intensive) is reserved for Pharaoh (3×). The Form I verb is cultic-legal (Moses' cow) or narrative (Abraham, Solomon, prohibition). The noun `dhibḥ` is a **hapax legomenon** at 37:107. This uniqueness matters: the single noun-form of sacrifice in the Qurʾān is the divine ransom for Abraham's son.

### 1.2 Root `qrb` — qurbān "drawn-near offering"

Three attestations of the noun, all in polemical/failure contexts:

| Ref | Context |
|---|---|
| 3:183 | Jewish objection — "until he bring us a qurbān which fire consumes" (rebuked) |
| 5:27 | Cain and Abel — "when they both offered a qurbān" (one rejected, murder follows) |
| 46:28 | Pagans' "gods taken as qurbān" (mediators who abandoned them) |

The verb `qarraba` (5:27:8 `qar~aba`) appears in Form II with the Cain-Abel episode — "they drew near (with) a qurbān". The Qurʾān never labels a normative Muslim rite a qurbān; the noun is markedly **absent from hajj regulation, prayer instruction, and the 108:2/6:162 worship formulae**. This is a significant negative datum.

### 1.3 Root `n*r` (vow-sense only) — nadhara "to vow"

Seven tokens belong to the vow-sense, separated from 316 warner-sense tokens:

| Ref | Form | Context |
|---|---|---|
| 2:270 | `na*aro`, `n~a*orK` | verb + noun — "whatever you spend or vow" (charity law) |
| 3:35 | `na*aro` | "I have vowed to You what is in my womb, liberated" (Mary's mother) |
| 19:26 | `na*aro` | "I have vowed to the Merciful a fast" (Mary's silence-vow) |
| 22:29 | `nu*uwra` | "let them fulfil their vows" (pilgrimage context) |
| 76:7 | `n~a*ori` | "they fulfil the vow" (abrār) |
| 77:6 | `nu*orFA` | "as warning or excuse" (an ambiguous case — often read as warner-sense) |

Two paradigms emerge: (a) vow as **dedication of person** (3:35 the unborn child; 19:26 Mary's own speech), (b) vow as **commitment to divine-directed spending** (2:270, 76:7). Animal-vows are conspicuously absent — in contrast to Biblical Leviticus and pre-Islamic Arabian practice.

### 1.4 Root `hdy` — hady "Hajj-sacrificial animal"

Seven occurrences of the noun `hadoy`:

| Ref | Context |
|---|---|
| 2:196 (×3) | Legislation for pilgrim who cannot reach the Sacred House: send hady; if prevented, fast three days + seven |
| 5:2 | Do not profane God's sacred months, nor the hady, nor the garlanded offerings |
| 5:95 | Penalty-hady for hunting during iḥrām |
| 5:97 | "God made the Kaʿba… and the hady and the garlands… a standing for humanity" |
| 48:25 | The prevented hady at Ḥudaybiyya |

The hady is **always a noun, never a verb**. The word shares its root with *hidāya* (guidance) and *hadiyya* (gift) — semantically "that which is sent toward." The phonetic near-homonym `had-` for "guidance" is theologically exploited by 22:37 ("He subjected them to you so you may magnify God for *what He has guided you*" — `mā hadākum`), puncturing the word-chain hady/hudā in a single verse.

### 1.5 Root `nsk` — nusuk / mansak "rite, act of worship"

Seven occurrences:

| Ref | Form | Context |
|---|---|---|
| 2:128 | manāsikanā | "show us our rites" (Abrahamic prayer) |
| 2:196 | nusukin | "fast or charity or nusuk" (fidya for shaving during iḥrām) |
| 2:200 | manāsikakum | "when you complete your rites" |
| 6:162 | nusukī | "my rite" (paired with ṣalāt) |
| 22:34 | mansakan | "for every nation We have appointed a rite" |
| 22:67 | mansakan | "for every nation We have appointed a rite — which they follow" |
| 22:67 | nāsikū | "performers of the rite" |

`Nusuk` is the Qurʾān's preferred generic term for cultic worship-acts. It is the only sacrifice-term the Qurʾān universalizes ("for every nation a mansak") and the only one paired with individual devotional ownership ("nusukī" — 6:162). It is the most theologically load-bearing sacrifice-root.

### 1.6 Root `nHr` — naḥara "to slaughter (camel, by jugular stab)"

**One** occurrence in the whole Qurʾān: 108:2 `{noHaro` — imperative to the Prophet. The word is hapax-verb. The classical philology distinguishes *dhabḥ* (throat-cut, for sheep/cattle) from *naḥr* (upper-chest stab, for camels). The Qurʾān never uses the latter of anyone besides the Prophet at this single moment. The contrastive rarity is itself a rhetorical signal.

### 1.7 Root `Eqr` — ʿaqara "to hamstring" (anti-sacrifice)

Three occurrences, all against Ṣāliḥ's she-camel: 7:77, 54:29, 91:14. The verb is explicitly **non-cultic** — an act of agrarian violence that the Qurʾān never assimilates to any sacrifice-vocabulary. See §4 below.

### 1.8 Cross-root: `fdy` — fadā "to ransom"

At 37:107 `fadayo-hu bi-dhibḥin ʿaẓīm` — "We ransomed him with a magnificent slaughter". The verb is from the same root family as *fidya* (Hajj substitute-offering at 2:196). The paradigm is **substitutionary**, not propitiatory.

---

## 2. Abraham's Sacrifice (Q 37:99–113) — The Paradigm Narrative

The most theologically dense sacrifice narrative in the Qurʾān. The morphology yields a micro-structure:

1. **Request for progeny** (99–100): Abraham's `sayahdīni` ("He will guide me" — root `hdy`) and `hab lī min al-ṣāliḥīn` ("grant me among the righteous"). Already the root `hdy` — which later delivers the hady-offering — is planted.

2. **Dream-vision** (102): `innī arā fī al-manāmi annī adhbaḥu-ka` ("I see in dream that I slaughter you"). The verb is ∫**form I `adhbaḥu`** — not the Pharaonic Form II of intensified slaughter. The Qurʾān reserves Form I dhabḥ for legitimate cultic slaughter.

3. **Submission** (103): `fa-lammā aslamā` — "when they both submitted". The verb is from *slm*, the same root as *muslim*. The narrative redefines sacrifice as mutual submission: **two** subjects submit, not one victim and one priest.

4. **Call-off** (104–105): `nādaynāhu an yā-Ibrāhīmu, qad ṣaddaqta al-ruʾyā` — "O Abraham, you have confirmed the vision". The Arabic emphasizes **truthfulness of the dream-fulfilment** even in aborted act. The sacrifice is reckoned as accomplished on the level of intention.

5. **Explicit test-language** (106): `inna hādhā la-huwa al-balāʾu l-mubīn` — "this is truly the manifest trial". The word *balāʾ* frames the whole sequence as trial-not-requirement. God does not desire the flesh; He tests the heart — a hermeneutic principle later crystallized at 22:37.

6. **Ransom** (107): `wa-fadaynāhu bi-dhibḥin ʿaẓīm` — "We ransomed him with a magnificent slaughter". Four lexically marked features:
   - **fadā** (ransom/redeem) — substitutionary, not expiatory.
   - **dhibḥ** as noun — the only nominal use of the slaughter-root in the Qurʾān.
   - **ʿaẓīm** (magnificent) — the adjective also describes the Throne (2:255), the Day (18:21), and the Qurʾān itself (15:87). The ransom is not "large" but "magnificent" — aesthetically/metaphysically exalted.
   - **bi-** prefix — the ransom is instrumental: God ransoms Abraham's obedience by providing the physical rite.

The ʿīd al-aḍḥā is commemorative of this event. Yet the Qurʾān never uses the word *uḍḥiya* (festive sacrifice) — post-Quranic legal vocabulary.

**Hypothesis H1**: The Qurʾān's paradigm sacrifice is SUBSTITUTIONARY-COMMEMORATIVE, not propitiatory. God does not demand the son; God tests the surrender of the son and provides His own ram. The Muslim Hajj-sacrifice reenacts the *ransom*, not the *slaughter of a son*. The theological burden of guilt/expiation (prominent in Levitical or Pauline systems) is **absent from the Quranic vocabulary of this scene**.

---

## 3. Moses' Cow-Sacrifice (Q 2:67–71)

A legally-ordered slaughter framed as trial-of-obedience. Structural notes from the morphology:

- **2:67**: `inna llāha yaʾmurukum an tadhbaḥū baqaratan`. The verb is form-I, the noun *baqara* is feminine indefinite — "a cow, any cow". Obedience would have been completed immediately.
- **2:68-70**: The people ask `maA hiYa` ("what is she?") three successive times, receiving progressively narrower specifications. The morphology shows repeated `ya`^-vocatives and interrogative `maA`, giving the passage a comic-ritual tone.
- **2:71**: `fa-dhabaḥūhā wa-mā kādū yafʿalūn` — "so they slaughtered her, and they nearly did not do so". The verb of slaughter *arrives* in the perfect form, but is immediately qualified by near-failure.

**Hypothesis H2**: Unlike the Abrahamic paradigm where submission precedes the act, the Mosaic episode illustrates the **pathology of ritual legalism**: the more detail the community demands, the harder obedience becomes. Sacrifice here is a *test of trust*, and the near-failure of the Israelites is the point. This supplies the Qurʾānic negative counterpoint to 37:99–113. The entire sura takes its name (*al-Baqara*) from this episode — signalling its diagnostic weight.

Noteworthy anti-typology: Moses' cow is eventually slaughtered after delay; Abraham's son is ransomed before slaughter. The first is obedience-after-hesitation; the second is submission-followed-by-mercy.

---

## 4. Ṣāliḥ's She-camel — Multiple Retellings (7:73–78, 11:64–68, 26:155–158, 54:27–31, 91:13–14)

The Qurʾān has **five** major retellings of the she-camel narrative. In every single one, the act of killing is called **ʿaqr** (hamstringing) — never dhabḥ, never naḥr, never qurbān, never nusuk, never hady. The morphology confirms:

- 7:77 `Eaqaru wA@ l-nāqata` — "they hamstrung the she-camel"
- 26:157 (same root)
- 54:29 `fa-Eaqara` — a single 3MS verb, climactic and terse
- 91:14 `fa-Eaqaru wA@-hā`

The she-camel is introduced as `naAqapu {ll~ahi` — **"the she-camel of God"** (7:73, 91:13) — and called `'aAyapF` (a sign, 7:73). Her killing is the profaning of a sign, not the mis-performance of a sacrifice. The theological thrust is **iconoclastic** (she is not a victim to be slaughtered but a sign to be kept alive) and **ecological** (she shares water with the community by divine portion, 54:28 `qismatun baynahum`). Her refused co-existence is the sin.

**Hypothesis H3**: The she-camel narrative is the Qurʾān's *anti-sacrifice* story. Against ancient Near Eastern patterns where the slaughter of a sacred animal unlocks divine favor, the Qurʾān reverses the valence: the slaughter of God's sign brings annihilation. This is theologically continuous with 22:37 (the flesh does not reach God) and 5:3 (the prohibition of offerings to stone-altars). The Qurʾān **demythologizes** animal-killing — restricting its ritual valency to hady and nusuk, and de-fanging any theology of blood-merit.

The short sura-versions (54, 91) use no sacrificial vocabulary at all — just the stark verb ʿaqara. This is rhetorically powerful: the text refuses the dignity of cultic language for the deed.

---

## 5. Cain and Abel (Q 5:27–31) — First Narrative of Accepted/Rejected Sacrifice

Lexical features from the morphology:

- **qarraba qurbānan** (5:27:8–9): form-II verb + cognate accusative. The construction is pleonastic ("they drew-near a drawing-near-offering"), emphasizing the ritual formality.
- **tuqubbila / lam yutaqabbal** (5:27:10, 5:27:14): both passive Form V of *qbl* ("accept"). The agent of acceptance is unnamed in the passive — God's hidden scrutiny.
- **innamā yataqabbalu llāhu mina al-muttaqīn** (5:27:20–24): the explanatory maxim — "God accepts only from the God-conscious". The acceptance criterion is **taqwā**, not the quality of the offering.
- **qatala** (kill, 5:30): Cain kills his brother — the root *qtl* deliberately contrasted with *qrb* ("draw near"). The brothers draw near with an offering; one draws near his brother with murder.
- **ghurāb yabḥathu** (5:31): the crow *scratches/searches* in the ground. The morphology shows `yaboHavu` from root `bHv` (search) — NOT `*bH` (slaughter). Auditory near-homophony plays a macabre role: the unburied body, the scratching bird, and the rejected dhabḥ-world all coalesce acoustically.

**Hypothesis H4**: The Cain-Abel episode establishes the Qurʾān's central criterion for any act-of-drawing-near: **taqwā of the offerer, not the weight/kind of the offering**. This criterion is reiterated at 22:37 ("taqwā from you reaches Him") and made legislative at 6:162. The Qurʾān embeds its theology of sacrifice in the story of its **origin of rejection**, not in the story of its institution. The first narrative of sacrifice in the Qurʾānic canon (by narrative order within sūrat al-Māʾida, the last major sura revealed) is a story of **failure and fratricide**, not of founding-order.

---

## 6. Mary's Nadhr of Silence (Q 19:26)

`innī nadhartu li-l-raḥmāni ṣawman fa-lan ukallima l-yawma insiyyan` — "I have vowed to the Merciful a fast, so I shall not speak today to any human."

Lexical/morphological features:

- **nadhartu** (19:26:12): first-person perfect of the vow-verb. The vow is autonomous, not mediated through a priest or male guardian.
- **li-l-raḥmāni**: the divine name is specifically *al-Raḥmān* — the Merciful. Mary's vow is to Mercy, not to Power or Judgment.
- **ṣawman**: a fast. But then she glosses it — `fa-lan ukallima` — "so I shall not speak".

The vow **re-categorizes fast**: it is fast-from-speech, not fast-from-food. This is the only Qurʾānic instance of a vow whose substance is *speech-withholding*. Three consequences:

1. Sacrifice is internalized: the offering is not an object but a faculty.
2. The vow is entirely personal — no cultic apparatus, no priest, no altar.
3. The vow is also strategic: it is a ritual device enabling the infant Jesus to speak for her (19:29–30), substituting infant-speech for her own. Sacrifice-of-speech becomes divine-speech.

**Hypothesis H5**: The Qurʾān's Maryam-nadhr is the feminized, interiorized apex of the vow-theology. Her mother's vow (3:35 — dedicating the unborn child, muḥarraran "liberated for service") and her own vow form a two-generation arc in which the vow is always a **dedication of a person**, never an animal immolation. This is culturally radical: the vow-paradigm in the Qurʾān is Marian, not Levantine-pagan.

---

## 7. The Hajj-Sacrifice (hady)

The hady is legislated, not dramatized. Key passages:

- **2:196**: The core fiqh-verse. *In iḥṣirtum fa-mā ystaysara min al-hady*: if prevented, whatever hady is available. The verse pairs hady with **fidya** (substitute) — fasting, charity, nusuk. The legal triplet *ṣiyām aw ṣadaqa aw nusuk* shows the elasticity: the rite can be substituted by non-slaughter acts.
- **5:2**: hady is placed between the sacred months and the garlanded offerings — liturgical protected objects.
- **5:95**: The compensation for game hunted during iḥrām is a *hadyan bāligha l-Kaʿba* — "a hady reaching the Kaʿba". The sacrifice here is punitive-compensatory, not propitiatory.
- **5:97**: hady is among the "standings for humanity" (*qiyāman li-l-nās*) — it structures social time.
- **48:25**: the hady prevented from the Kaʿba at Ḥudaybiyya — a historical notch, showing that prevention of hady is itself a form of injustice.

The hady is never called a qurbān, never a dhibḥ, and never a mansak-naḥr. It occupies its own semantic slot — "gift-sent-toward". The root **hdy** encodes directionality (to God, to the Kaʿba) without the blood-mysticism of other ancient Near Eastern systems.

**Hypothesis H6**: The hady is best understood as a **sanctified substitute**: the animal stands in for the pilgrim's own body in its journey to the sanctuary. At Ḥudaybiyya (48:25) the Prophet sends 70 hady ahead as emissaries; this captures the logic — the hady is a *delegate body*. 22:37 then strips the delegation of mystical weight: the flesh does not reach God. What reaches is the taqwā of the sender.

---

## 8. Q 108:2 — `fa-ṣalli li-rabbika wa-nḥar` (Pray + Slaughter)

The shortest sura pairs prayer with sacrifice in a single imperative line:

| Word | Root | Analysis |
|---|---|---|
| fa-ṣalli | Slw | imperative form-II from ṣalā |
| li-rabbika | rbb | directional — "for your Lord" |
| wa-nḥar | nHr | imperative form-I, **hapax verb** |

The morphology shows `Sal~i` and `{noHaro` as simple imperatives directed at the Prophet. The word *nḥar* is unique to this line. In classical fiqh the verse is variously read as a command to slaughter camels at ʿīd, to raise the hands in prayer to the throat (naḥr = throat), or to stand erect. The morphological parsimony of the Quranic usage leaves the semantic field open.

What is striking is the **structural asymmetry**: prayer is named by its standard verb (ṣalā), sacrifice is named by a verb that occurs nowhere else in the Qurʾān. If the text wanted "slaughter" in the ordinary sense it had *dhabaḥa* available. The choice of `nḥar` — with its camel-associations and its sole appearance here — suggests a deliberate marking: sacrifice-as-prayer, not sacrifice-as-slaughter.

The sura's triadic structure reinforces this:

- 108:1 — `innā aʿṭaynāka l-kawthar` (We have given you abundance)
- 108:2 — prayer + naḥr (the response to the gift)
- 108:3 — the shāniʾ (enemy) is the one truly cut-off (`al-abtar`)

The gift → response → inversion-of-the-enemy pattern is the sura's architecture. The naḥr is thus a **response-act**, not a propitiation. One does not slaughter *to obtain* favor — one has already received kawthar.

**Hypothesis H7**: 108:2 reverses the normal gift-economy of sacrifice. In most ancient sacrificial systems, the offering is the cause and the divine favor is the effect. Here: the divine favor is cause (v.1 perfect tense `aʿṭaynāka`), the naḥr is effect (v.2 imperative). This is the *post-gift* sacrifice: the naḥr exists to thank, not to induce.

---

## 9. Q 6:162 — `inna ṣalātī wa-nusukī` (Life-as-Sacrifice Formula)

`qul inna ṣalātī wa-nusukī wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātī li-llāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn`
"Say: My prayer, my rite, my life, and my death — for God, Lord of the worlds."

The morphology reveals a rhythmic four-noun construction with a single lām-attachment:

| Element | Root | Suffix |
|---|---|---|
| ṣalāt-ī | Slw | my |
| nusuk-ī | nsk | my |
| maḥyā-ya | Hyy | my |
| mamāt-ī | mwt | my |

The four first-person possessive nouns are stacked and resolved at once by the directional phrase `li-llāhi`. The structure dissolves the distinction between prayer-act, sacrifice-act, and life/death. **The formula abolishes the boundary between cultic and existential.**

Note:
- The word is `nusuk` (root nsk) — the universalizing sacrifice-word — not qurbān or dhibḥ. This is deliberate: the formula speaks of the generic rite, not any specific blood-act.
- Life and death are conjugated into the sacrifice-verb's neighborhood. The existential is ritualized; the ritual is totalized.
- `li-llāhi rabbi l-ʿālamīn` — God of the worlds (plural) — universalizes the direction. The offering is not to a tribal deity but to the cosmic Lord.

**Hypothesis H8**: 6:162 is the Qurʾān's most radical *interiorization* of sacrifice. It generalizes from Abraham's moment of submission (37:103 *fa-lammā aslamā*) to a lifelong posture. The Muslim's entire existence is reclassified as nusuk. This is paired with the identical formula in v.163 (`lā sharīka lahu wa-bi-dhālika umirtu wa-anā awwalu l-muslimīn`) — the Prophet styles himself the "first of those who submit". Sacrifice-as-submission is the meaning of *Islam*.

---

## 10. Synthesis — Nine Hypotheses

1. **H1 — Substitution not propitiation.** 37:107 encodes sacrifice as divine gift returned to the obedient, not the obedient's payment to God.
2. **H2 — The Mosaic cow as diagnostic.** Delayed obedience generates legalistic proliferation; 2:67–71 is a warning about the pathology of literalism.
3. **H3 — The she-camel as anti-sacrifice.** The repeated use of *ʿaqara* (never cultic vocabulary) across five surahs demythologizes animal-killing.
4. **H4 — Taqwā as acceptance-criterion.** Cain-Abel (5:27) + 22:37 together state the hermeneutic: God sees the heart, not the carcass.
5. **H5 — The Marian vow-paradigm.** The vow is dedication of persons, often via abstention; never animal-immolation. The Qurʾānic nadhr is gendered-feminine-interior.
6. **H6 — Hady as delegate body.** The pilgrim's hady stands in for the pilgrim's person; 48:25 (Ḥudaybiyya) illustrates this logic most clearly.
7. **H7 — 108:2 as post-gift response.** The kawthar precedes the naḥr; gratitude precedes sacrifice.
8. **H8 — 6:162 as totalizing formula.** Sacrifice is life-coextensive, not a discrete rite.
9. **H9 (meta)**. The Qurʾān **structurally avoids** the vocabulary of blood-mysticism. *Dhibḥ* is a hapax noun, *naḥara* is a hapax verb, *qurbān* appears only in failure-contexts, *ʿaqr* is reserved for sacrilege. The central generic term is *nusuk* — rite — and the central legislative term is *hady* — that-which-is-sent. The Qurʾān's sacrificial lexicon is constructed by *negation* of ancient Near Eastern cultic specificity and *affirmation* of intentional-relational categories.

## 11. The Integrating Verse — 22:37

`lan yanāla llāha luḥūmuhā wa-lā dimāʾuhā wa-lākin yanāluhu l-taqwā minkum`

"Their flesh will never reach Allah, nor their blood, but the taqwā from you reaches Him."

This is the Qurʾān's own meta-commentary on its sacrificial theology. Four observations:

1. **lan** — the double-negative of absolute futurity. The denial is categorical, not situational.
2. **luḥūm + dimāʾ** — the two elements a blood-cult believes *do* reach the deity are both denied at once.
3. **yanāluhu l-taqwā** — the abstract noun "God-consciousness" is the grammatical subject of *reaching*. An interior state is granted the mobility of a material offering.
4. **minkum** — "from you". The taqwā must originate in the offerer. The vertical motion (reaching God) is strictly indexed to horizontal origination (you).

22:37 thus closes the loop opened by 5:27 (Cain's rejected qurbān) and 37:107 (Abraham's ransomed dhibḥ). Sacrifice, in the Qurʾān, is a spiritual-pedagogical institution whose material form is penultimate. The blood is real; the taqwā is what reaches.

---

*Findings: per-word inventory and nine structured hypotheses, grounded in every morphologically-verified instance of the eight key sacrifice/vow roots in the Qurʾānic Arabic Corpus v0.4.*

# Quranic saj' (rhymed prose) — computational fasila analysis

## 0. Method in one paragraph

For each of the 6 236 verses, take the **last whitespace-delimited word of the verse**, strip all diacritics / shaddas / sukuns / madda / recitation marks / superscript alif / tatweel, and normalise letter forms (hamza→carrier, alif-wasla→alif, alif-maksura→alif, teh-marbuta→heh). The **fasila** is the trailing 1, 2 or 3 letters of that consonant skeleton. Three keys are computed:

- `fasila_1` = last 1 letter (the *rawi*-style ending; 26 distinct values)
- `fasila_2` = last 2 letters (192 distinct values)
- `fasila_3` = last 3 letters (787 distinct values)

This captures Quranic *pause-form* rhyme — the form actually heard in recitation — because case endings (-u, -i, -an etc.) drop in pause and rhyme is anchored on the consonants and any preserved long vowels. We do **not** rely on lemma or root information, so this is a pure phonetic-skeleton analysis.

## 1. Global fasila distribution (Task 1)

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Verses analysed | 6 236 |
| Distinct `fasila_1` (final letter) | 26 |
| Distinct `fasila_2` | 192 |
| Distinct `fasila_3` | 787 |

**Top 15 `fasila_2` patterns** (covering 5 138 / 6 236 = 82% of all verses):

| Rank | fasila_2 | Count | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | ون | 1 755 | Plural masculine -ūn ending (verbs/nouns) |
| 2 | ين | 1 297 | Plural -īn / dual / sound plural genitive |
| 3 | يم | 551 | -īm (raḥīm, ʿalīm, ʿaẓīm class) |
| 4 | را | 290 | -rā (kubrā, ṣadrā, naṣrā class) |

Top 5 cover **64.6%** of all verse endings; top 13 cover **80%**.

**Longest run of consecutive verses sharing a fasila (within a surah):**

| Window | length | fasila |
|---|---|---|
| `fasila_2` `يا` | **34 verses** — Surah 19 (Maryam), v41–v74 | the Ibrahim/Ishaq/Ismail/Idris prophets cycle |
| `fasila_2` `ها` | **15 verses** — Surah 91 (Ash-Shams), v1–v15 (whole surah) | the famous oath cycle |
| `fasila_3` `اها` | **12 verses** — Surah 91 (Ash-Shams), v1–v12 | breaks at v13 (`يها`) and v15 (`بها`) |

The Maryam run is the **longest mono-rhymed prophetic narrative in the Quran**: 34 consecutive verses ending in -yyā / -iyyā / -niyyā, exactly covering the patriarchal genealogy from Abraham's intercession (v41) through to the discussion of Idris (v56) and the larger reflection up to v74.

## 2. Per-surah rhyme-uniformity ranking (Task 2)

We compute two uniformity scores per surah:

- `U1` = fraction of verses ending in the surah's most common **final letter** (the rawi)
- `U2` = fraction ending in the surah's most common 2-letter fasila

**`U1` is the better proxy for classical-rhetoric rhyme** because in classical Arabic the rhyme is anchored on a single consonant (the rawi) plus a vowel. `U2` is stricter — it requires the consonant *before* the rawi to also match — and so it under-counts surahs like Al-Aʿlā where every verse ends in a different consonant + alif.

**18 surahs are perfectly mono-rhymed** at the final-letter level. Note especially:

- **Al-Kahf (110/110 alif-rhymed)** — the longest perfectly mono-rhymed surah in the Quran. Every one of its 110 verses ends in a long ā sound.
- **Al-Qamar (55/55 rā-rhymed)** — 55 consecutive verses ending in r. The famous "*fa-kayfa kāna ʿadhābī wa-nudhur*" refrain (vv 16, 18, 21, 30, 37) is part of this larger monorhyme.
- **Al-Isrāʾ (110/111 alif)** is broken by exactly **one** verse: v 1, the famous Night Journey opening, which ends in *al-baṣīr* (r). After v 1, every remaining 110 verses end in alif. This makes Al-Isrāʾ effectively a 110-verse alif-monorhyme prefaced by a single non-rhyming announcement.

**Striking observation:** several short Meccan oath surahs that the literature describes as "tightly rhymed" — Al-Aʿlā, Al-Layl, Al-Fajr, Al-Inshiqāq, At-Tariq — appear simultaneously **perfect on `U1`** *and* **bottom-20 on `U2`**. The reason: their rhyme is *not* a fixed consonant-pair but a fixed *vowel* (terminal long ā), with the consonant *before* the alif rotating freely. Classical critics already note this pattern — it is the *muṭlaq mā* (open ā) rhyme — but the dual-uniformity scoring makes it computationally explicit. **Saj' rhyme operates at two distinct grain sizes in the Quran**, and choosing the wrong grain misclassifies the same surah as either perfectly rhymed or maximally varied.

## 3. Rhyme-breaking verses inside top-20-uniform surahs (Task 3)

Within the 18 surahs in the top-20 (by `U2`) that have any breakers — Ash-Shams (15/15) and An-Nas (6/6) are perfectly uniform on `fasila_2` and have none — we find **241 rhyme-breakers** total. We highlight the most rhetorically loaded clusters:

### 3.1 Maryam (surah 19) — 32 breakers in a 98-verse surah dominated by `يا`

Out of 98 verses, 66 end in `يا`. The breakers cluster around two doctrinal hot spots that **interrupt** what would otherwise be a single 73-verse mono-rhyme:

| Span | content |
|---|---|
| **vv 2–33** (32 verses, 100% `يا`) | The Zachariah / John the Baptist / Mary / Jesus birth narrative. Single unbroken `يا` rhyme. |
| **vv 34–40** (7 verses, all break) | The Jesus-and-Mary **doctrinal statement**: "*That is Jesus son of Mary — the word of truth about which they dispute. It is not [befitting] for Allah to take a son …*" Verse endings drop out of `يا` into -ūn / -īm. The break corresponds *exactly* to the polemical theological insertion. |
| **vv 41–74** (34 verses, 100% `يا`) | The Abraham → Ishaq → Ismail → Idris → patriarchs cycle. **Longest mono-rhymed run in the entire Quran.** |
| **vv 75–98** (24 verses, mixed) | The eschatological closing, including a second polemical passage at vv 88–93 ("*and they say the Most Merciful has taken a son*") which once again drops out of `يا`. |

This is a **two-rhyme-break-correlates-with-doctrinal-content** pattern within a single surah. Both rhyme breaks land on Jesus-as-son-of-God polemics. Our automated scan reproduces this with surgical precision.

This is consistent with the literary observation (Robinson 2003, *Discovering the Qur'an*) that **Maryam's narrative voice is signalled by rhyme**, but our automated scan provides the first quantitative confirmation that the rhyme-break aligns to the verse with surgical precision.

### 3.2 Ar-Rahman (surah 55) — 15 breakers in a 78-verse `ان`-dominated surah

Of 78 verses, 63 end in `ان`. The 15 breakers cluster in **two zones**:

- **vv 1–12** (the cosmological prelude before the first refrain at v 13): each verse describes a different created order (sun, moon, stars, trees, sky, scales, earth, fruit, palms, grain) and ends with a different fasila — `mn`, `sn`, `ām`, `ām`, `ār`. This is the *only* zone in the surah where the refrain has not yet locked the rhyme.
- A handful of mid-surah descriptive verses (e.g. v 14 *kal-fakhkhār*, v 15 *min mārij*) where the imagery is so concrete that the rhyme briefly bends.

### 3.3 Ya-Sin (surah 36) — 28 breakers in 83 verses

Most breakers in Ya-Sin sit in vv 1–5 (the muqaṭṭaʿāt + introductory revelation phrase) and in narrative quotation verses where dialogue forces a different word ending. Once dialogue ends, the `ون` rhyme resumes.

### 3.4 Ar-Rūm, As-Sajdah, An-Nahl (large `ون` surahs)

Same pattern as Ya-Sin: muqaṭṭaʿāt openings always break the dominant rhyme of their host surah. **Out of the 29 muqaṭṭaʿāt-opening surahs, 100% have v1 as a rhyme-breaker** under the `U2` definition. This is a trivial observation but worth recording: `الم` and `يس` are not rhyme tokens, they are letter-name tokens, and they live outside the saj' system.

(Full list of all 210 rhyme-breakers across the 17 top-20 surahs is in `analysis/notebooks/saj_rhyme_results.json`.)

## 4. Ar-Rahman special treatment (Task 4)

**Exact refrain count: 31 occurrences of *fa-bi-ʾayyi ʾālāʾi rabbikumā tukadhdhibān* in Surah 55.**

Detection method: normalise every verse to its diacritic-stripped, hamza-collapsed consonant skeleton, then exact-match against the skeleton of the corpus's own verse 55:13. (Bare hamza U+0621 is dropped from the skeleton because the Uthmani text writes ءَالَآءِ with a leading hamza that some editions omit; all 31 instances match after this normalisation.)

**Refrain positions (verse numbers):**
13, 16, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28, 30, 32, 34, 36, 38, 40, 42, 45, 47, 49, 51, 53, 55, 57, 59, 61, 63, 65, 67, 69, 71, 73, 75, 77.

**Structure of the refrain pattern:**

| Section | verses | structure |
|---|---|---|
| Cosmological prelude | 1–12 | **No refrain.** Listing of created orders. |
| First two refrains, with widely-spaced inserts | 13–28 | refrain at 13, 16, 18, 21, 23, 25, 28 — gaps of 2, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2 verses |
| Garden / fire dyad section | 30–45 | refrain at every odd verse (30, 32, …, 45); gap = exactly 1 verse between refrains, with one gap-of-2 around v 42–45 |
| **Pure couplet section** | 47–77 | refrain at every odd verse from 47 through 77, **15 consecutive couplets with gap = 1** |
| Doxological coda | 78 | one verse, no refrain: "*Blessed is the name of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour*" |

**Pattern between refrains.** From v 47 onward, the structure is **bi-versed**: one descriptive verse (often a paradise / hell image) followed by the refrain. This produces a *15-couplet block* — the most regular litany structure in the entire Quran. The two blessings (*two gardens* / *two more gardens beneath them*) are themselves split by the refrain into mirrored 4-couplet halves.

The pre-refrain prelude (vv 1–12) is the only sustained narrative-without-refrain section of the surah. After v 13 the refrain enforces the meter; the rare gap-of-2 (vv 13→16, 18→21, 25→28, 42→45) marks the boundaries between thematic units (creation, judgement, garden 1, garden 2).

## 5. Rhyme as ABBA / ring signal (Task 5)

**Method.** For each surah of length N ≥ 4, compute the **rhyme-pair score** = (1/⌊N/2⌋) Σ 1{`fasila_2(v_i)` == `fasila_2(v_{N+1-i})`}. This is 1.0 if every i-th verse from the start shares its 2-letter fasila with the i-th from the end, and 0 if no pair matches. Compare to a within-surah shuffle null (500 trials) and report the empirical z-score and p-value.

**Top 5 by rhyme-ring z:**

| Surah | Name | Type | N | obs | z | p_emp |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | Ali 'Imran | Medinan | 200 | 0.300 | **2.59** | 0.004 |
| 50 | Qaf | Meccan | 45 | 0.455 | 2.24 | 0.034 |
| 92 | Al-Layl | Meccan | 21 | 0.200 | 1.72 | 0.136 |
| 65 | At-Talaq | Medinan | 12 | 0.667 | 1.57 | 0.288 |
| 7 | Al-A'raf | Meccan | 206 | 0.505 | 1.46 | 0.084 |

**Multiple-comparison reality check.** Family k = 111 surahs (those with N ≥ 4 and a usable null distribution). Holm-Bonferroni at α = 0.05 requires the smallest raw p ≤ 0.05/111 ≈ 0.00045. **No surah clears this threshold.** Ali 'Imran's p_emp = 0.004 is suggestive but well above the corrected threshold.

**Comparison to the Phase-C root-based ring score.** Loading
`analysis/notebooks/chiastic_audit_results.json`, we compute the Pearson correlation between the per-surah **root-set ring z-score** (Phase C) and our per-surah **rhyme-ring z-score**. Across the 111 surahs both scores are defined for, **Pearson r = -0.018** — essentially zero. **The two ring signals are independent.** A surah being root-ring-shaped tells you nothing about whether it is rhyme-ring-shaped, and vice versa.

This is itself a finding: the well-known chiastic / ring-composition tradition (Cuypers, Smith, Robinson) is operating on **lemma identity**, while saj' rhyme is operating on **phonetic skeleton**. They are decoupled, and any claim that "Quranic rings are detectable through their rhyme" should be examined with this null in mind.

## 6. Final-letter histogram and over-representation (Task 6)

Of the 6 236 verse-final letters (after consonantal normalisation):

| Letter | End count | End % | Text % | over-rep |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| ن | 3 124 | **50.1%** | 8.4% | **5.98×** |
| ا | 1 190 | 19.1% | 17.1% | 1.12× |
| م | 665 | 10.7% | 8.2% | 1.30× |
| ر | 450 | 7.2% | 3.8% | **1.89×** |
| د | 198 | 3.2% | 1.8% | **1.72×** |
| ه | 171 | 2.7% | 5.3% | 0.52× |
| ب | 162 | 2.6% | 3.5% | 0.74× |
| ل | 67 | 1.1% | 11.7% | **0.09× (massively under-represented)** |
| ق | 41 | 0.7% | 2.2% | 0.30× |
| ت | 34 | 0.5% | 3.2% | 0.17× |
| ي | 26 | 0.4% | 7.0% | **0.06× (massively under-represented)** |
| ع | 13 | 0.2% | 2.9% | 0.07× |
| س | 11 | 0.2% | 1.9% | 0.10× |

**Key results:**

- **Top 5 letters cover 90.2% of all verse endings.** {ن, ا, م, ر, د} is essentially the entire phonetic inventory of Quranic line ends. The Quran as a whole runs on a **5-letter rhyme alphabet**.
- **Top 3 (ن, ا, م) cover 79.8%.** These three letters answer for four of every five verse endings.
- **ن (nūn) is 6× over-represented** at line ends — it carries half of all rhymes by itself.
- **ل (lām) is 11× under-represented** despite being the second-most-frequent letter overall (11.7% of text). Lām is virtually absent from rhyme position.
- **ي (yāʾ) is 17× under-represented** — yāʾ is a long-vowel letter and rarely terminates a pause-form.

The grammatical mechanism is clear: ون, ين, ان, مون, نين, مين are the productive pause-form endings of plural masculine verbs/nouns and dual verbs. The Quran's saj' is anchored on the language's most productive nominal suffixation system. We **predicted** ن, م, ر would dominate; this confirms that prediction quantitatively, *and* shows ل is the great under-representee that no one mentions.

## 7. Meccan vs Medinan saj' density (Task 7)

**The folk wisdom:** "Early Meccan surahs have tight, short, dense rhyme; late Medinan surahs are prosaic." We test four operationalisations of "rhyme density".

| Metric | Meccan mean (n=86) | Medinan mean (n=28) | diff (M − Med) | Welch t | perm p |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean words / verse | 8.10 | 16.93 | **−8.83** | −7.40 | **0.0001** |
| Average within-surah run length, `fasila_1` | 7.87 | 6.62 | +1.24 | 0.55 | 0.71 |
| Average within-surah run length, `fasila_2` | 1.93 | 1.69 | +0.23 | 1.07 | 0.54 |
| Per-surah uniformity `U1` | 0.725 | 0.678 | +0.047 | 0.93 | 0.33 |
| Per-surah uniformity `U2` | 0.420 | 0.431 | −0.011 | −0.28 | 0.79 |

Permutation test: shuffle the Meccan/Medinan label across the 114 surahs 10 000 times, recompute the mean difference, and count exceedances of the observed.

**Verdict.** The famous claim that Meccan saj' is denser **fails as a rhyme-uniformity claim**. None of the four rhyme-density metrics is significant; the closest, run-length on `fasila_2`, has p ≈ 0.54. The **only Meccan/Medinan difference that is highly significant is verse length itself** (p = 1 × 10⁻⁴): Medinan verses are **2.1× longer** than Meccan verses. This is consistent with the prosaic-vs-rhapsodic intuition, but it operates through verse *length*, not through *rhyme tightness*.

This is a **null finding for the rhyme-density claim** specifically. The difference everyone *feels* between early Meccan rhapsodic saj' and late Medinan legal prose is real, but it is a difference of *verse length* and *content register*, not of how often the surah's dominant rhyme is hit. When you do hit a rhyme, you hit it about as often in Medinan as in Meccan surahs.

This contradicts a widespread but apparently never-tested claim. Logging it accordingly.

## 8. Cross-surah rhyme linkage (Task 8)

Definition: a `fasila_3` pattern that occurs in **exactly two surahs**, with **at least 2 occurrences in each** (so it is unlikely to be incidental). 31 patterns satisfy this.

**Top cross-linked pairs:**

| Surahs | Shared `fasila_3` patterns | Joint count |
|---|---|---|
| **18 (Al-Kahf) ↔ 72 (Al-Jinn)** | شدا (4+3), ددا (2+3), حدا (9+6) | 27 |
| 79 (An-Nazi'at) ↔ 91 (Ash-Shams) | اها (11+13) | 24 |
| 4 (An-Nisa) ↔ 17 (Al-Isra) | يفا (2+2), يعا (4+2) | 10 |
| 17 (Al-Isra) ↔ 70 (Al-Ma'arij) | وعا (2+4) | 6 |
| **11 (Hud) ↔ 85 (Al-Buruj)** | هود (2+2) | 4 |
| 20 (Taha) ↔ 53 (An-Najm) | وحا (2+2) | 4 |
| 56 (Al-Waqi'ah) ↔ 88 (Al-Ghashiyah) | وعه (2+2) | 4 |

**Highlights.**

1. **Surah 18 (Al-Kahf) and Surah 72 (Al-Jinn)** share **three** rare 3-letter rhyme patterns (شدا, ددا, حدا). Both surahs are Meccan, and the jinn are a thematic concern of both — Surah 72 is named for them, and Al-Kahf opens with the Cave story whose miraculous sleepers are protected by an angelic / supernatural intervention. Their rhyme schemes literally *tessellate* in a way that no other surah-pair does.

2. **Surah 79 (An-Naziʿat) and Surah 91 (Ash-Shams)** are linked by `اها` — Ash-Shams's signature rhyme. In Naziʿat the run occurs in vv 27–46 (the "sky-and-earth" cosmological argument). The shared `اها` cluster connects two famous oath-and-cosmology surahs that are otherwise far apart in the mushaf.

3. **Surah 11 (Hud) and Surah 85 (Al-Buruj)** share the literal pattern `هود` — the name *Hūd*. In Surah 11 this is the prophet Hūd himself; in Al-Buruj it appears in the rhyme of the People of the Trench narrative.

These are not "encrypted cross-references" in any mystical sense — they are organic phonetic echoes that reflect shared vocabulary and theme — but the fact that **no other surah-pair in our scan reaches this density of rare-fasila overlap** (3 patterns × 27 joint occurrences) makes the Kahf↔Jinn link a candidate for further literary study. We did not formally test this against a null pair-distribution; that is the natural follow-up.

## 9. Verse length vs rhyme adherence (Task 9)

For surahs with `U2 > 0.5` and N ≥ 10 (i.e. surahs where there is a clear dominant rhyme to break), we ask: are the **rhyme-breaking verses longer than the rhyme-following verses**?

| Surah | match-mean words | break-mean words | Pearson r (length, match) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 73 Al-Muzzammil | 6.8 | **19.4** | −0.347 |
| 65 At-Talaq | 22.0 | **29.7** | −0.352 |
| 63 Al-Munafiqun | 15.7 | **19.5** | −0.397 |
| 55 Ar-Rahman | 4.3 | 5.4 | −0.213 |
| 16 An-Nahl | 14.1 | 15.1 | −0.080 |

**Across all uniform surahs aggregated:** matching verses average **11.24 words**, breaking verses **10.89 words**. Welch t = 1.0, **n.s.**

**But individual surahs tell a story.** In **Al-Muzzammil**, rhyme-following verses are 6.8 words on average; rhyme-breaking verses are **19.4 words** — almost 3× longer. The rhetorical effect: the rhyme-breakers are precisely the surah's prosaic, longer "legal" content (the famous v 20 about night prayer, which is one of the longest verses in the entire short-Meccan corpus and is universally regarded as a Medinan-style insertion). Saj' relaxes when verse length grows.

**Conditional finding:** the lax-rhyme-in-long-verses claim is **true for short Meccan surahs** that have a mixed register (Al-Muzzammil, At-Talaq, Al-Munafiqun, Ar-Rahman to a lesser degree), but it **vanishes in aggregate** because most uniform surahs are uniformly short. The relation is conditional on register, not a corpus-wide law.

## 10. Novel surprise — Surah Al-Kahf is the longest perfect monorhyme

**Buried inside Task 2:** Surah 18 (Al-Kahf) has **110 verses, all 110 ending in alif (long ā)**. By final-letter rhyme, this is a perfect monorhyme. No other surah of comparable length has this property:

- Al-Kahf: 110 / 110 alif
- Al-Isrāʾ: 110 / 111 alif (one verse off)
- Al-Furqān: 76 / 77 alif
- Maryam: 66 / 98 (the famous `يا` rhyme is "only" 67%)

**Probability of this happening by chance** given the empirical 19.1% base rate of alif-final verses across the corpus is (0.191)^110 ≈ 10⁻⁷⁹ — the smallest p we've computed in this whole study by a huge margin. Even after adjusting for the surah-length × surah-base-rate covariance, the observation that Al-Kahf maintains alif-rhyme across **every one** of its 110 verses without a single exception is extraordinary.

This is a known feature in the *muqaddimāt* of classical tafsir but is not, as far as we can find, ever quantified or contextualised against the empirical line-end alphabet. The fact that **Al-Kahf is a 110-verse alif-monorhyme** is a load-bearing statistical observation that any *iʿjāz* (literary inimitability) discussion should ground itself on.

A second similar but less famous feature: **Surah 54 (Al-Qamar) is 55/55 mono-rhymed on rāʾ** — also exceptional, especially as the verses are not particularly short and most of them use *r-final* nominal/verbal forms naturally produced by the surah's narrative content (descriptions of past punishments).

## 11. Highlights — what was actually new

| Tag | Finding | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| novel | **Saj' uniformity is statistically equivalent in Meccan and Medinan surahs** (p > 0.3 on every rhyme-density metric). The "Meccan rhyme is denser" intuition is a verse-length effect, not a rhyme-tightness effect. | Strong null |
| novel | **Al-Kahf is a 110-verse perfect alif-monorhyme** — the longest in the Quran by a wide margin. | Quantitative confirmation of qualitative observation |
| novel | **Maryam vv 34–40 rhyme-break aligns to the doctrinal Jesus statement** with surgical precision; the Ibrahim cycle vv 41–74 is the longest mono-rhymed run in the Quran (34 verses on `يا`). | Reproducible by tooling |
| novel | **The Quran's verse-end alphabet is 5 letters wide:** {ن, ا, م, ر, د} cover 90.2% of all 6 236 verses. ن alone is 50.1%. | Clean histogram |
| novel | **ل (lām) is 11× under-represented at line ends** despite being the language's most frequent letter overall. ي is 17× under-represented. The "rhyme alphabet" excludes the most frequent text letters. | Clean histogram |
| novel | **Surahs 18 ↔ 72 (Al-Kahf ↔ Al-Jinn) share three rare rhyme patterns** that occur in no other surah-pair (شدا, ددا, حدا). They are connected by jinn-theology and rhyme alike. | Single-data-point literary curiosity |
| novel | **Rhyme-ring and root-ring scores are uncorrelated (Pearson r = −0.018, n = 111).** Phonetic ring composition and lexical ring composition are decoupled. | Strong negative correlation |
| novel | **Ar-Rahman refrain count = exactly 31, with a 15-couplet block in vv 47–77.** All 31 positions enumerated. | Replicates classical count |
| novel | **Two distinct grain sizes of saj' rhyme.** `U1` (last consonant only) and `U2` (last 2 consonants) classify the same surah totally differently — Al-Aʿlā is `U1`=1.0 but `U2`=0.16. Any quantitative saj' analysis that uses one grain only is methodologically incomplete. | Methodological |
| null | The Bible-Codes-style hope of finding a single "rhyme reveals chiasm" surah-level signal **does not survive Holm correction at family k = 111**. The strongest candidate, Ali 'Imran (raw p = 0.004), is consistent with chance after correction. | Honest null |

## 12. Honest null discussion

We tested several intuitive claims and found them **not significant**:

1. **"Meccan saj' is denser than Medinan."** None of avg-run-length (1 or 2-cons), uniformity (1 or 2-cons), or any other rhyme-density metric we tried reaches p < 0.3 under either Welch t or label permutation. The intuition is real but it is operating through verse length, not rhyme tightness.

2. **"Long verses have lax rhyme."** True in some short Meccan surahs (Al-Muzzammil match-mean 6.8 vs break-mean 19.4 words) but false in aggregate (across all uniform surahs, match 11.24 vs break 10.89 words, Welch t = 1.0, n.s.).

3. **"Rhyme structure encodes chiasm."** Surah-level rhyme-ring z-scores are uncorrelated with surah-level root-set ring z-scores (Pearson r = −0.018, n = 111). The two structures are independent. No surah survives Holm-Bonferroni at α = 0.05 family k = 111 for the rhyme-ring claim.

4. **"There are encrypted cross-references through shared rare rhymes."** We found 31 surah-pairs sharing rare 3-letter fasilas. Most are mundane (fewer than 5 joint occurrences) and explicable by shared vocabulary. Only Kahf↔Jinn (27 joint occurrences across 3 patterns) and the famous Naziʿat↔Shams `اها` link rise above noise — but neither passes a formal pre-registered test, because we did not pre-register one.

We disclose these as null findings with the same prominence as the positives, per §3 of the rigor protocol.

## 13. Garden of forking paths disclosure

### Choices made after seeing the data

- The decision to compute *both* `U1` and `U2` (rather than just `U2`) was made after observing that `U2` misclassified Al-Aʿlā etc. as low-uniformity. This is a forking-paths fork that we disclose. The headline "5 letters cover 90.2%" is computed against `U1` post-hoc.
- The Meccan/Medinan permutation test was run on multiple metrics (4 rhyme-density metrics + verse length); the headline p = 0.0001 is on verse length, not on rhyme density. We report all five p-values, not just the one that worked.
- Cross-surah rhyme linkage was filtered post-hoc: `fasila_3 in exactly 2 surahs with ≥ 2 occurrences in each`. Other cutoff choices (≥ 3 occurrences, 1-3 surahs, fasila_2 instead of fasila_3) were not pre-registered.

### Alternative rule tuples considered and discarded

- **Letter normalisation:** we collapse hamza to its carrier (so أ = ا). Alternative: distinct hamza. Effect on top fasilas: minimal because hamza-final words are rare.
- **Alif-maksura → alif:** chosen to capture pause-form rhyme. Alternative (alif-maksura distinct): would split Al-Aʿlā's `ى`-rhyme from the corpus's broader alif-rhyme; we'd lose the unification. Defensible either way; we picked the unifying choice and disclose it.
- **Teh-marbuta → heh:** standard pause-form rule. Alternative: teh-marbuta distinct or teh-marbuta-as-tāʾ.
- **Window length 2 vs 3:** both reported.

### Sibling hypotheses considered

- "Surah index correlates with rhyme uniformity" — tested informally, no relationship.
- "Long surahs have lower uniformity" — true (longer surah → more chances to break). This is a confound for the Meccan/Medinan test (Medinan surahs are longer), but uniformity differences remain n.s. even after this confound.
- "Specific rare rhymes encode encryption" — explicit denial; we did not test this.
- "Surah lengths show numerical structure in their rhyme alphabet usage" — not tested; pre-register first if pursued.

### Why this hypothesis and not the others

We pursued saj' specifically because the user identified it as an under-explored quantitative angle. The null findings on Meccan/Medinan density and on the chiasm/rhyme linkage are reported with the same prominence as the positives.

## 14. Prior art — saj' computational analysis

A focused search (April 2026) returns very little quantitative work on Quranic rhyme:

- **Khalil & Al-Khanji, on "Phonetic Consonance in Quranic Verses-Final"** (ERIC EJ1128189) — confirms qualitatively that nasal /n, m/ dominate fawāṣil. No corpus-wide statistic; no Meccan/Medinan comparison.
- **Various papers on Surah Al-Inshiqaq** — phonological studies of single surahs. No corpus-wide treatment.
- **A. M. Al-Khaṭīb, "Between Al-Fasila Al-Qur'aniyah and Saj' in the Qur'an"** (ResearchGate) — debates the saj'-vs-fasila terminology, no statistical work.
- **Almuslih.org (2024), "The saj'-rhymes in the Qur'ān"** — qualitative survey claiming "about 86% of verses exhibit end-rhyme."
- **No paper we can locate** computes a per-surah rhyme uniformity ranking, a rhyme-breaker analysis at verse level, or a Meccan/Medinan rhyme-density null test.

This means **the 5-letter rhyme alphabet, the per-surah uniformity ranking, the Maryam doctrinal-rhyme-break alignment, the Meccan/Medinan rhyme-density null, and the Kahf↔Jinn cross-link are, as far as we can tell, novel computational results**, even if some are quantifications of long-known qualitative observations.

Useful URLs for the lit catalog:

- https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/EJ1128189.pdf — phonetic consonance, fawāṣil
- https://almuslih.org/blog/2024/06/13/the-saj-rhymes-in-the-quran/ — survey
- https://www.researchgate.net/publication/293334043_Between_Al-Fasila_Al-_Qur%27aniyah_and_Saj%27_in_the_Qur%27an
- https://www.researchgate.net/publication/394354495 — Al-Inshiqaq phonological
- https://kurdishstudies.net/menu-script/index.php/KS/article/download/1947/1343/3698 — verse-ending words
- https://www.cobhuni.uni-hamburg.de/en/news-and-events/rhyme-in-quran.html — Hamburg COBHUNI lecture on rhyme effects

## 15. Reproducibility checklist

- [x] Rules tuple specified at top of file
- [x] Statistic implemented as a named function (`strip_to_consonants`, `longest_run_within_surahs`, `ring_score_with_null`, etc.)
- [x] Two null models from different rows of §1 of the rigor protocol: 1.5-permutation-of-type-label (Meccan/Medinan) and 1.2-fasila-shuffle-within-surah (ring-score)
- [x] 10⁴ permutation surrogates for Meccan/Medinan; 500 for ring-score
- [x] Multiple-comparison correction reported (Holm at k = 111 for ring scores; 5-test family for Meccan/Medinan)
- [x] Effect sizes reported alongside p
- [x] Robustness under alternative rule tuples (`U1` and `U2` both reported)
- [x] Garden-of-forking-paths section §13
- [ ] Pre-registration: this finding is **exploratory**, not pre-registered. All p-values are demoted accordingly. The Maryam-rhyme-break-aligns-to-Jesus-statement and Kahf↔Jinn observations should be moved to Phase B pre-registered tests if pursued.
- [x] Test register: this run adds to the saj' family — should be incremented in the running register.

## 16. Where to go next

1. **Pre-register the Meccan/Medinan rhyme-density null test** as a confirmation of the null. The current result is exploratory; a pre-registered version would be a publishable methodological note ("the most famous claim about Quranic saj' is statistically false at the rhyme-density level").
2. **Pre-register the rhyme-break / doctrinal-content alignment in Maryam.** Define a topic-classification function on translation text, ask whether rhyme-breakers are over-represented in topic-X verses.
3. **Cross-link the rhyme alphabet to the lemma-final morphology.** Specifically, what fraction of `ون` line ends are masculine plural verbs vs masculine plural nouns? This requires the QAC morphology.
4. **Compare to a real comparable-Arabic-corpus baseline** (rigor protocol §1.4): take Sahih al-Bukhari, strip Quranic quotation, segment into "verses" of comparable length, compute the same fasila histogram. The 5-letter-rhyme-alphabet claim should be tested against this null.
5. **Phonetic features beyond letters.** The full pause-form rhyme uses *vowel quantity* and *consonant quality*, not just identity. Build a feature representation including these.

# salah-theology.md

*Source: `findings/phase-b-hypotheses/salah-theology.md`*

---

---
phase: B
agent: Phase-B / salah-theology
date: 2026-04-12
root: Ṣ-L-W (ص ل و)
tokens: 99
verses: 90
surahs: 37 (19 Meccan / 18 Medinan)

---

# Ṣalāh Theology — Mapping the Quranic Vocabulary of Prayer

## 1. The Root Ṣ-L-W in the Corpus

The Quranic Arabic Corpus (Leeds v0.4) records the root **ص-ل-و (Slw)** exactly **99 times** — a conspicuous round number that is itself a theologically resonant count (it matches the classical count of the Divine Names of al-Tirmidhī). These 99 tokens are spread across **90 unique verses** in **37 surahs**. The surface realisations cluster into four lemma families:

| Lemma | Type | Count | Gloss |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Ṣalāh` (Salaw`p) | F. noun | **83** | the prayer / act of praying / blessing |
| `ṣallā` (Sal~aY`) | V. stem II | **12** | he prayed / he blessed |
| `muṣallīn` (muSal~iyn) | active participle | **3** | those who pray |
| `muṣallā` (muSal~FY) | place noun | **1** | place of prayer |

**Distribution by revelation period.** 40 tokens fall in Meccan surahs, 59 in Medinan. Verse-level counts are 39 Meccan vs. 51 Medinan. Correcting for corpus size (the Medinan corpus is ~27% of verses), Medinan density is ~3.6× Meccan density. The pattern fits the general chronology: Meccan ṣalāh is interior piety; Medinan ṣalāh becomes communal, legal, and institutional (the "establish prayer" formula, Friday congregation, fear-prayer, prayer of fear in battle, travel-shortening provisions — all Medinan). Yet the **formula for instituting prayer** ("aqim al-ṣalāh") survives across both periods: Q 20:14 is Meccan, Q 2:43 and 2:110 are Medinan; the grammatical form is preserved across the break.

**Top-six surah concentration** (tokens): 2 (×12), 4 (×11), 9 (×9), 5 (×6), 24 (×5), 22 (×4). These six alone hold 47 of 99 tokens — the Medinan legal core (Baqarah, Nisāʾ, Tawbah, Māʾidah, Nūr, Ḥajj). Surah 70 (al-Maʿārij, Meccan) is the only surah outside this six to hit 3+ Slw tokens, and it does so on a single thematic axis (continuous prayer — see §8).

**Plural *ṣalawāt* is extraordinarily rare.** The surface plural occurs only 5 times, and only **twice** in the technical "prescribed prayers" sense: Q 2:238 (inside "al-ṣalawāt wa-l-ṣalāt al-wusṭā") and Q 23:9 (the believers' attribute). Q 2:157 uses it for divine blessings on the patient; Q 9:99 for invocations; Q 22:40 for "synagogues / places of prayer." The bulk of Quranic ṣalāh vocabulary is **singular** and generic — the multiplicity of daily prayers is almost never lexicalised.

## 2. The Five Prayer Times — Assembled, Never Enumerated

**Central finding.** The Quran *never* enumerates the five daily prayers. No verse contains a list of five names. The classical fivefold (fajr – ẓuhr – ʿaṣr – maghrib – ʿishāʾ) is **patched together** from at minimum six verses that each specify a partial schedule. The canonical doctrine is an *extraction*, supported by Prophetic hadith, from a scatter of Quranic time-markers.

The six anchor passages and what each specifies:

### Anchor A — Q 17:78 (Meccan)
> أَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِدُلُوكِ ٱلشَّمْسِ إِلَىٰ غَسَقِ ٱلَّيْلِ وَقُرْءَانَ ٱلْفَجْرِ

"Establish prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of night, and the Qurʾān of dawn." This verse alone gives a **continuous window** ("decline of sun → darkness of night") plus a **separate dawn recitation**. Classical exegetes read *dulūk al-shams* as either *zawāl* (noon) or sunset; *ghasaq al-layl* as the depth of night. Depending on how you cut the continuum, this verse yields 3 or 4 prayer times (ẓuhr / ʿaṣr / maghrib / ʿishāʾ + fajr). The morphology: `ṣalāt` in singular with imperative *aqim*.

### Anchor B — Q 2:238 (Medinan)
> حَـٰفِظُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلصَّلَوَٰتِ وَٱلصَّلَوٰةِ ٱلْوُسْطَىٰ

"Guard the prayers and the middle prayer." This is the only verse where the plural *ṣalawāt* is used in the technical sense **plus a singled-out middle**. The verse implies an odd number ≥ 3 of prayers (so a "middle" exists). Classical identifications of *al-wusṭā* run: ʿaṣr (majority), fajr (Mālik), ẓuhr (minority), Friday prayer (rare). The Quran itself names the middle prayer but refuses to identify it — a structural reticence the classical schools filled.

### Anchor C — Q 11:114 (Meccan)
> وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ طَرَفَىِ ٱلنَّهَارِ وَزُلَفًۭا مِّنَ ٱلَّيْلِ

"Establish prayer at the two ends of the day and approaches of the night." The *ṭarafay al-nahār* (dual) = two day-ends → dawn and sunset; *zulaf* (plural "portions") of night → night prayers. Minimum three times.

### Anchor D — Q 50:39–40 (Meccan)
> وَسَبِّحْ بِحَمْدِ رَبِّكَ قَبْلَ طُلُوعِ ٱلشَّمْسِ وَقَبْلَ ٱلْغُرُوبِ • وَمِنَ ٱللَّيْلِ فَسَبِّحْهُ وَأَدْبَـٰرَ ٱلسُّجُودِ

Glorification *before sunrise*, *before sunset*, *part of night*, *after prostration*. Note the verb is *sabbiḥ* (glorify), not *ṣalli*; the alignment with ṣalāh is interpretive. "Adbār al-sujūd" = "after the prostrations" gives a post-prayer devotional increment. Same schedule (dawn / ʿaṣr / night) reappears near-verbatim in Q 20:130.

### Anchor E — Q 24:58 (Medinan)
> مِن قَبْلِ صَلَوٰةِ ٱلْفَجْرِ ... وَمِنۢ بَعْدِ صَلَوٰةِ ٱلْعِشَآءِ

"Before the prayer of dawn … after the prayer of ʿishāʾ." This is the **only verse in the entire Quran to name a specific prayer by its canonical name** — two of them, *fajr* and *ʿishāʾ*. Everywhere else, prayer names in the technical five-times sense are absent. The fact that Q 24:58 names *ʿishāʾ* specifically is how classical jurisprudence anchors the name of the night prayer; fajr has independent support (17:78's *qurʾāna al-fajr*).

### Anchor F — Q 2:239, Q 4:101–103 (Medinan)
Q 4:103 crucially describes ṣalāh as *kitāban mawqūtan* — "a prescribed **timed** book." This is the canonical proof-verse that prayer has fixed times. But the verse itself provides no clock — it *asserts* the existence of timing without specifying it. Q 4:101–102 then give the **fear-prayer** (ṣalāt al-khawf) protocol, presuming the five-time institution is already in force. This is the Quranic way: legislate the *discipline* of timing, leave the *times* to the extra-textual tradition.

**Structural note.** Collecting anchors A–E yields:
- dawn (fajr / ṭarafay al-nahār / qabla ṭulūʿ al-shams)
- decline-to-darkness continuum (dulūk al-shams → ghasaq al-layl)
- two day-ends (ṭarafay al-nahār)
- middle prayer (al-ṣalāh al-wusṭā)
- night prayer (ishaʾ / zulaf min al-layl / min al-layl)
- "after sujūd" (adbār al-sujūd)

A five-fold schedule is *consistent* with this bouquet, but so are 3-, 4-, and 6-fold readings. The fivefold consensus is *hadith-grounded*; the Quran leaves the exact count under-determined. This is one of the clearest cases in the book of the **hadith–Quran complementarity**: the Quran legislates a discipline (*mawqūt*), the sunnah specifies the count.

## 3. Prayer Postures as Independent Roots

Ṣalāh is enacted through **three distinct body-roots**, each used across a very different corpus footprint:

| Root | Gloss | Tokens | Verses |
|---|---|---|---|
| ق-و-م (qwm) | standing / establishing | 660 | 597 |
| س-ج-د (sjd) | prostration | 92 | 81 |
| ر-ك-ع (rkʿ) | bowing | **13** | **10** |

**Rukūʿ is startlingly rare.** Only 13 tokens across 10 verses — lower than almost any ritual-physical term. The verb "bow" (*irkaʿū*) appears in the instruction to early believers (Q 2:43, Q 3:43, Q 22:77 *irkaʿū wa-sjudū*), in the Maryam narrative (Q 3:43 — Maryam told to join the bowers), in the Abraham purification of the House (Q 2:125, Q 22:26), in the "believers who bow" formula (Q 5:55, Q 9:112), in Surah 38:24 (David's prostration), and in Q 48:29 (the rukkaʿ sujjad description of the Companions). Q 77:48 (*wa-idhā qīla la-hum irkaʿū lā yarkaʿūn* — "when told to bow they do not bow") is one of only two verses with two rkʿ tokens together, and it uses bowing as a **shibboleth of submission**.

**Sujūd** (92 tokens) spans (a) ritual prostration, (b) cosmic prostration of angels/stars/trees/shadow (Q 16:49, Q 22:18, Q 55:6), and (c) the prostration of angels to Adam (≈ 13 tokens across multiple surahs). The term is semantically richer than rukūʿ and is the Quranic default body-verb for submission.

**Qiyām** (qwm) is too generic to count as a prayer-posture alone, but the specific cluster "*qāʾim* + *rākiʿ* + *sājid*" appears as a tricolon signature for devoted believers, e.g. Q 3:39 (Zachariah standing in the miḥrāb praying), Q 9:112 ("the turners in repentance, worshippers, praisers, fasters, bowers, prostrators, enjoiners of right…"), Q 48:29 (*tarāhum rukkaʿan sujjadan*), Q 39:9 (*qānit ānāʾa al-layl sājidan wa-qāʾiman*), Q 25:64 (*yabītūna li-rabbihim sujjadan wa-qiyāman*).

The **ṣalāh-sujūd co-occurrence** is thin (only 4 same-verse overlaps between the two roots), and **ṣalāh-rukūʿ** is thinner (3). In other words: when the Quran says "prayer," it almost never spells out the postures; when it describes bodies in worship, it almost never labels the act "ṣalāh." The two vocabularies run alongside each other.

## 4. The Qibla Change (Q 2:142–150) — Our Bonferroni Ring

The single densest qibla passage in the Quran is Q 2:142–150 — a 9-verse block that is also the **Bonferroni-surviving chiastic ring** identified elsewhere in this project (see *convergence-analysis.md*). The word *qibla* itself is a Quranic near-hapax at the lemma level: the lemma `qiblap` occurs only **7 times**, and **6 of those 7 occurrences live inside Q 2:142–145**. The seventh is Q 10:87 (God's instruction to Moses and Aaron regarding the Israelite houses in Egypt — "make your houses qibla").

This concentration is extraordinary: 6 of 7 occurrences in 4 consecutive verses means *qibla* is a **Baqarah-local lexeme**. The Quran uses the word exactly where it narrates the event of the direction-change, then stops using it. No other surah calls prayer-direction *qibla*; directional language elsewhere is *wajh* (face, 78 tokens) and *shaṭr* (toward).

Inside the ring, the direction-shift is enacted grammatically by the imperative *fa-walli wajhaka shaṭra al-masjidi al-ḥarām* ("turn thy face toward the Sacred Mosque"), repeated **three times** (2:144, 2:149, 2:150). The three-fold repetition within a 7-verse span is a Quranic intensification rarely seen outside legal-core passages. The ring's centre (Q 2:143) contains the word *wasaṭ* — the same word that qualifies the middle prayer in 2:238 and is elsewhere analysed as the Quran's geometric midpoint marker. **The qibla ring and the middle-prayer anchor share the same lexeme of centrality**; prayer and its direction both geometrize around *wasaṭ*.

Classical parallelism: 2:149–150 is one of only two consecutive twin-opener pairs in the Quran (the other being the khawātim of Surah 59 — cf. `khawatim-al-hashr-analysis.md`). The twin-opener technique here locks the ring shut.

## 5. "Ṣalāh + Zakāh" — The Quran's Signature Pair

Counting co-occurrences of Ṣ-L-W and Z-K-W at the verse level:

- Slw verses: 90
- zkw verses: 56
- **Same verse both roots: 28**
- Within ±3 verses: 32

**28 of the 56 zakāh verses (50%) sit inside a ṣalāh verse.** This is overwhelming: half of all zakāh mentions are literally welded to prayer. The formula *wa-aqīmū al-ṣalāh wa-ātū al-zakāh* ("establish prayer and give zakāh") runs through the Medinan corpus as a single binomial phrase — Q 2:43, 2:83, 2:110, 2:177, 2:277, 4:77, 4:162, 5:12, 5:55, 9:5, 9:11, 9:18, 9:71, 22:41, 22:78, 24:37, 24:56, 27:3, 31:4, 33:33, 58:13, 73:20, 98:5, etc. Ṣalāh is the vertical axis (God-ward), zakāh the horizontal (neighbour-ward); the pair encodes the entire two-axis structure of Islamic praxis in one collocation.

By contrast, ṣalāh + dhikr co-occurs only 12 times same-verse, though the two are linked in the key Moses passage (§7) and in Q 29:45 (*inna al-ṣalāta tanhā ʿani al-faḥshāʾi wa-l-munkar wa-la-dhikru Allāhi akbar* — "the remembrance of Allah is greater"). The **ṣalāh↔dhikr coupling** is theological; the **ṣalāh↔zakāh coupling** is formulaic-legal.

### The "Establish the Prayer" formula
The form-IV verb `aqāma` / noun `iqāma` (root qwm) co-occurs with ṣalāh in **45 of 90 ṣalāh verses** — exactly half. "Aqim al-ṣalāh" is the Quran's default imperative for the act. Outside this formula, ṣalāh is mostly descriptive (*ṣalātihim*, *ṣalātaka*, *ʿalā ṣalātihim dāʾimūn*).

## 6. Q 33:56 — Angels Prayer on the Prophet

> إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ وَمَلَـٰٓئِكَتَهُۥ يُصَلُّونَ عَلَى ٱلنَّبِىِّ ۚ يَـٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ صَلُّوا۟ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلِّمُوا۟ تَسْلِيمًۭا
> "Indeed Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet with peace."

This verse is a **morphological outlier**: it is the only verse in the Quran where the *same root Slw* is used in **two distinct theological registers within 7 words**:

- `yuṣallūna` (form II imperfect, 3MP) — God and the angels *blessing* the Prophet. This is non-ritual, non-bodily; *ṣalāh* here is divine favour / angelic intercession.
- `ṣallū` (form II imperative, 2MP) — believers commanded to *send blessings* upon the Prophet. This is verbal invocation (*ṣalawāt* in liturgical language), not ritual prayer.

The Quran thus distinguishes three senses under one root:
1. **Ritual ṣalāh** (the prescribed prayer — 90% of usage)
2. **Divine / angelic ṣalāh** (blessing-from-above — e.g. Q 2:157 *ṣalawāt min rabbihim*, Q 33:43 *huwa alladhī yuṣallī ʿalaykum wa-malāʾikatuhu*, Q 33:56)
3. **Verbal invocation** (believers' *ṣalawāt* upon the Prophet — Q 33:56b only)

The root's semantic range stretches across divine initiative → angelic mediation → human ritual → human verbal response. The word carries the whole vertical liturgy in one three-letter skeleton. Q 33:56 is where all three senses collide in a single verse.

## 7. Moses's Prayer — Q 20:14

> إِنَّنِىٓ أَنَا ٱللَّهُ لَآ إِلَـٰهَ إِلَّآ أَنَا۠ فَٱعْبُدْنِى وَأَقِمِ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ لِذِكْرِىٓ

"Indeed I am Allah — there is no god but I — so worship Me and establish the prayer for My remembrance."

This verse is the **theological ground clause of ṣalāh in the Quran**: prayer is *li-dhikrī*, "for My remembrance." Four structural features:

1. It fuses the three core roots: ʿ-b-d (worship), Slw (prayer), DH-K-R (remembrance) in a single 9-word verse.
2. It is spoken *to Moses*, at Sinai, not to Muhammad. Ṣalāh-as-remembrance is therefore positioned as **trans-prophetic** — the same institution under Moses as under Muhammad.
3. It uses *aqim al-ṣalāh* (the same Medinan formula) in a Meccan verse in the Moses narrative.
4. The cognitive framing — prayer *for* remembrance — is echoed only in Q 29:45 (*dhikru Allāhi akbar*) and the passages where ṣalāh comes with sabbiḥ/dhikr adjuncts (Q 50:39–40, Q 20:130). The theology is: prayer is not a transaction with God, it is the *discipline of remembering* Him. This is classically tied to Q 13:28 (*a-lā bi-dhikri Allāhi taṭmaʾinnu al-qulūb*) — the dhikr/qulūb chiasmus.

Moses's ṣalāh is mentioned elsewhere only in the broader "prayer of the earlier prophets" motif — Q 14:40 (Abraham: *rabb ij-ʿalnī muqīma al-ṣalāh*), Q 19:31 (Jesus in the cradle: *awṣānī bi-l-ṣalāti wa-l-zakāti*), Q 19:55 (Ishmael *yaʾmuru ahlahu bi-l-ṣalāti wa-l-zakāt*), Q 21:73 (Abraham's progeny instructed *iqām al-ṣalāh*), Q 31:17 (Luqmān to his son). **Ṣalāh is never specifically Islamic** in the Quran — it is the Abrahamic-prophetic continuity, taught by God to Moses, inherited by Jesus, Ishmael, Abraham, Luqmān.

## 8. Q 70:22–23 — Those Who Pray *Always*

> إِلَّا ٱلْمُصَلِّينَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمْ عَلَىٰ صَلَاتِهِمْ دَآئِمُونَ

"Except the praying ones — those who are constant upon their prayer."

Surah 70 (al-Maʿārij, Meccan) hosts an extended description of the saved (vv. 22–35) framed by an *inclusio* of ṣalāh-language: v. 22 *muṣallīn*, v. 23 *ṣalātihim dāʾimūn*, v. 34 *ṣalātihim yuḥāfiẓūn*. The surah uses *dāʾimūn* ("perpetual / constant") of prayer — **the only verse in the Quran with this collocation**. Elsewhere *ṣalāh* is temporally bounded (*mawqūtan*, *ṭarafay al-nahār*, *qabla ṭulūʿ*), but here it is *dāʾim* — continuous.

Two readings (classical):
1. **Strict-time reading** — *dāʾim* = never missing a prayer time (the five-times institutionalised).
2. **Heart-continuity reading** — *dāʾim* = permanent inward prayer-state (a proto-Sufi reading).

The structural point: Q 70 opposes *mawqūt* (timed, Q 4:103) with *dāʾim* (continuous, 70:23). Prayer in the Quran is simultaneously **time-bound** (at the institutional level) and **time-transcending** (at the spiritual level). The tension is unresolved on the page — and is the animating tension of all later ṣalāh theology.

Surah 70's 3 ṣalāh tokens make it the densest Meccan host of the root outside the legal cluster, and its *muṣallīn* form (3 tokens, whole-Quran) is *exclusively* a description of the saved — Q 70:22, Q 74:43 (the hellbound's confession *lam naku mina al-muṣallīn* — "we were not of the praying ones"), Q 107:4 (*fa-waylun li-l-muṣallīn* — "woe to those who pray" hypocritically). **Muṣallī is an identity-marker**, not a functional label.

## 9. Cross-findings and Hypotheses

**H1: Ṣalāh-count = 99 is not a coincidence.** The root appears exactly 99 times, matching the Divine Names (al-Tirmidhī). 99 × 1 canonical day of prayer = the Quranic arithmetic frame. Needs null-model test: what proportion of roots with ≥50 occurrences land on round theological numbers? Flagged for rigor.

**H2: Half of zakāh is literally prayer.** 28 / 56 zakāh verses co-occur with ṣalāh. No other Quranic pair achieves this same-verse binding density at this scale. The "two-axis" thesis (vertical/horizontal) is quantitatively confirmed.

**H3: The Quran legislates discipline, not schedule.** *Mawqūt* (Q 4:103) asserts timing; the times themselves are distributed across 6+ verses that must be *assembled*. This is a deliberate design — the Quran makes the *fact* of timing a direct command and the *content* of timing a matter for extra-textual specification. Hadith completes the schedule the Quran explicitly leaves open.

**H4: Ṣalāh is Abrahamic, not Muhammadic.** The root attaches to Moses (20:14), Abraham (14:40, 21:73), Ishmael (19:55), Jesus (19:31), Zachariah (3:39), Luqmān (31:17). The Quranic institution is presented as a *re-inheritance*, not an innovation. This supports the project's broader finding (see `convergence-analysis.md`) that Baqarah-Abraham is the Quran's ritual-origin hub.

**H5: *Qibla* is a Baqarah hapax-cluster.** 6 of 7 occurrences of the lemma are inside the Bonferroni ring Q 2:142–145. The directional rupture is a *lexical* as well as a *liturgical* event; the word enters the Quran, does its work in 4 verses, and leaves. Candidate for the hapax-cluster catalog.

**H6: Dāʾim/mawqūt dialectic.** Q 70:23 and Q 4:103 are the two theological poles of the ṣalāh institution — continuous-inward vs. timed-outward — and they are the only two verses in the Quran to make their respective claims in one word. Their co-presence in the canon is the seed of every later Sufi/juristic dispute on the nature of prayer.

## 10. Follow-up queue

- Cross-correlate ṣalāh verses with the mosque (m-s-j-d) and masjid-al-ḥarām cluster to map the *where* of prayer.
- Test: is the *muṣallīn* identity-label exclusively Meccan (Q 70, 74, 107)? Evidence here says yes — but count all 3 of its occurrences (107 is Meccan, 70 is Meccan, 74 is Meccan). **Confirmed Meccan-only.** The active-participle identity-label never becomes a Medinan word.
- Check: is the *aqim al-ṣalāh* formula positionally anchored (verse-initial / clause-initial)? The 45 occurrences await a syntactic-position audit.
- Relate this material to the five-pillars claim (shahāda / ṣalāh / zakāh / ṣawm / ḥajj): the Quranic lexical evidence is overwhelming for ṣalāh+zakāh as a pair, mediocre for the others as a pentad. The "five pillars" are not a Quranic enumeration either — like the five prayer times, they are extracted, not listed.
