# Scientific Foreknowledge (iʿjāz ʿilmi) — Honest Audit

## 0. Framing

The modern *iʿjāz ʿilmi* ("scientific miracle of the Quran")
movement traces to Maurice Bucaille's *La Bible, Le Coran et la
Science* (1976), and was amplified by Keith L. Moore's 1980s
editions of *The Developing Human*, by Harun Yahya (Adnan Oktar)'s
mass-market publishing operation, and by the Egyptian geologist
Zaghloul al-Naggar's television programmes. The movement claims
that the Quran contains specific, non-trivial descriptions of
natural phenomena that were unknown to 7th-century Arabia and
have since been confirmed by modern science. If true — and as
the user framed it: "stated it existed but never existed back
then, or told the future" — this would be a genuinely novel
epistemic claim worth taking seriously.

The critical literature (Pervez Amirali Hoodbhoy, *Islam and
Science*, 1991; Taner Edis, *An Illusion of Harmony*, 2007;
Aron Ra; and academic Qur'anic studies scholars such as
Nidhal Guessoum) has responded that *iʿjāz ʿilmi* is a
methodologically flawed form of **concordism** — the practice of
picking a modern scientific fact, then scanning a scripture for
any verse that can be read as saying it, with unbounded
freedom to stretch semantics. This is structurally identical
to the fault McKay, Bar-Natan, Bar-Hillel & Kalai (1999)
diagnosed in the Bible Codes: enough degrees of freedom will
let you find any pattern you are looking for in any
sufficiently long text.

This audit applies the project's statistical-rigor protocol
(`docs/statistical-rigor-protocol.md` §4) — in particular the
red-flag list for post-hoc rule selection, undisclosed counting
conventions, cherry-picked temporal horizon, and refusal to
enumerate siblings — to each of the twelve canonical claims.
For each, we steelman the apologetic reading, state the
7th-century background knowledge the Quran would have been
competing with, state what modern science actually says, and
give an honest verdict on a six-level scale.

One calibrating note at the outset. The premise that 7th-century
Arabia was a scientific vacuum is historically false. Mecca was
a long-distance trade hub connecting Sassanid Iraq, Byzantine
Syria, and Yemen (itself in contact with India). Syriac-speaking
Christians were established in Najrān, al-Ḥīra, and Mesopotamia,
and they had translated Galen and Aristotle. Jewish tribes in
Medina — Banū Qurayẓa, Banū al-Naḍīr, Banū Qaynuqāʿ — had
rabbinic learning rooted in the Mishna and Talmud. Zoroastrian
Persia had its own natural philosophy. Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry
is rich in astronomical, zoological, and meteorological imagery.
The claim "the 7th-century Arab could not have known X" must be
tested against *this* background, not against a fictional
isolated desert.

The second calibrating note is the **survivor-bias filter**. The
apologetic literature quotes the ~12 verses that look prescient
after modern science caught up. It is silent about the verses
that look scientifically odd by the same method of literal
reading: sperm produced between the backbone and ribs (Q 86:6-7),
the sun setting in a muddy spring (Q 18:86), stars as
missiles against eavesdropping jinn (Q 67:5, 15:18), seven
layered heavens (Q 67:3) and matching seven earths (Q 65:12),
a worm eating Solomon's staff (Q 34:14). A symmetric audit must
include these. Concordism cannot have it both ways — either
figurative reading is legitimate for both sides or for neither.

---

## 1. Embryology (Q 23:12-14, 22:5, 39:6, 76:2)

### 1.1 The text

> Q 23:12-14: "And certainly We created the human from a drawing
> (*sulāla*) of clay. Then We made him a drop (*nuṭfa*) in a
> firm lodging. Then We made the drop a clinging/clot (*ʿalaqa*),
> then We made the clinging-thing a morsel (*muḍgha*), then We
> made the morsel bones (*ʿiẓām*), then We clothed the bones
> with flesh (*laḥm*), then We brought him into being as another
> creation."
>
> Q 22:5: "…from dust, then from a drop, then from a clot, then
> from a morsel formed and unformed…"
>
> Q 39:6: "…creating you in the wombs of your mothers, creation
> after creation, in three darknesses…"
>
> Q 76:2: "…We created the human from a drop, mingled
> (*amshāj*)…"

### 1.2 Apologetic reading (Bucaille 1976; Keith Moore 1982)

The Quran describes embryonic development in a sequence
(drop → clot/leech → morsel → bones → flesh) that matches
modern embryology: zygote → implantation → somite stage →
skeletal development → myogenesis. Moore called it "a remarkably
accurate description" given "the state of knowledge at the time."

### 1.3 7th-century background

The staged description of embryonic development is **Galen's**,
with Arabic names. *De Semine* (2nd c. CE) describes:
(i) seminal fluid ("foam"); (ii) blood-filled /
clotted stage; (iii) flesh-like stage; (iv) formed limbs. Galen
was widely translated into Syriac by the 6th century and
circulated in the medical schools of Jundishapur and Edessa.
The Talmud (Niddah 25a, Yevamot 69b) offers a broadly similar
staged account, with the *golem* (unformed mass) corresponding
closely to *muḍgha*. Hellenistic medicine had reached the
eastern Mediterranean centuries before the Quran.

The specific apologetic selling-point — that *ʿalaqa* means
"leech-like" and matches the shape of a ~24-day-old embryo — is
a 1980s reading that required **polysemy-selection**. The root
ʿ-l-q covers "cling, suspend, stick, attach, leech." Classical
tafsir (Ṭabarī, Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī) overwhelmingly read
*ʿalaqa* as "blood clot" (*qiṭʿat damm jāmid*) — the same sense
Galen had. The "leech" polysemy was foregrounded only after
Moore was shown a ~24-day embryo micrograph in the 1980s. This
is a textbook **red flag** per stats-rigor protocol §4:
post-hoc rule selection from an unenumerated polysemy space.

### 1.4 Modern embryology

Bones and muscle do not develop sequentially. Both are
derived from the same mesenchymal tissue, and myogenesis is
essentially concurrent with — not subsequent to — osteogenesis.
The Quranic image "we made the morsel bones, then we clothed
the bones with flesh" is a sequential picture that does not
match embryology as actually understood post-1950. Several
peer-reviewed critiques of Moore's endorsement
(e.g. Saleem 2002; Aziz 2012) note this.

### 1.5 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING KNOWLEDGE + partially inaccurate**

The staged framework is Galenic. The polysemy-shopping on
*ʿalaqa* is concordism. The sequential bones-then-flesh
picture is actually incorrect. This is the single most-cited
*iʿjāz* claim, and it fails both historical (pre-existing)
and scientific (partial mismatch) tests.

---

## 2. Cosmic Expansion (Q 51:47)

### 2.1 The text

> *wa-l-samāʾa banaynāhā bi-aydin wa-innā la-mūsiʿūn*
> "And the heaven — We built it with *aydin*, and indeed We
> are *mūsiʿūn*."

### 2.2 Apologetic reading

*mūsiʿūn* = "expanders" → foretells Hubble's 1929 observation
of galactic recession and cosmic expansion.

### 2.3 Linguistic check

*mūsiʿūn* is an active participle from the root w-s-ʿ. The root
covers: "to be wide, spacious, capacious; to encompass; to have
abundance; to make room for." Participles in Arabic are stative
by default, not progressive. Classical commentators read the
verse various ways:

- Ibn ʿAbbās: "We are its *expanders*" in the sense of "We have
  made it vast" (completed, stative).
- Ṭabarī: reads *mūsiʿūn* as "capable, abundant in power"
  (*aghniyāʾ qādirūn*) — treating the participle as an attribute
  of God's power, not a cosmological claim.
- Qurṭubī: offers both "we made it vast" and the abundance reading.
- Ibn Kathīr: "We made it spacious above the earth."

The "progressive expansion" reading — *We are currently
continuing to expand it* — is not attested in the classical
tafsir tradition. It appeared in the 20th century, after
Hubble.

### 2.4 Modern cosmology

Cosmic expansion is real (Hubble 1929, type-Ia SN 1998 on
acceleration). The metric expansion is of space itself, not
of "the heaven" understood as a dome.

### 2.5 Verdict — **AMBIGUOUS**

The Arabic *permits* a progressive reading. It does not
*require* one, and classical readers did not choose it. That
the modern apologist can find one polysemy of a multivalent
participle that matches modern cosmology is exactly the
forking-paths fault. A fair test would be: does the Quran
describe expansion *using a form that grammatically specifies
ongoing process* (e.g. an imperfective verb
*innā la-nūsiʿuhā* "we are expanding it")? No. It uses the
stative participle. Apologists score this as a hit; a fair
grader scores it as AMBIGUOUS with a tilt toward
retrofitting.

---

## 3. Big Bang / Ratq-Fatq (Q 21:30)

### 3.1 The text

> *a-wa-lam yara alladhīna kafarū anna al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa
> kānatā ratqan fa-fataqnāhumā, wa-jaʿalnā min al-māʾi kulla
> shayʾin ḥayy*
> "Have those who disbelieved not seen that the heavens and the
> earth were a joined/sealed thing (*ratq*), then We split
> them (*fataqnā*), and We made from water every living
> thing?"

### 3.2 Apologetic reading

*Ratq* = primordial singularity. *Fatq* = Big Bang. Therefore
the Quran teaches inflationary cosmology.

### 3.3 Classical tafsir (the reading the apologetic movement
suppresses)

- **Ibn ʿAbbās:** the sky was sealed, producing no rain; the
  earth was sealed, producing no vegetation. God opened the
  sky with rain and the earth with plants.
- **Mujāhid, ʿIkrima, Qatāda, Ibn Zayd:** same rain-release
  reading.
- **Ṭabarī:** lists the above as the dominant view; notes a
  minority view that heaven-and-earth were a single mass that
  was separated.
- **Qurṭubī:** same majority rain reading.

The immediate context — "and We made from water every living
thing" — is consistent with the rain-release reading and
disconnected from any cosmological singularity. The structural
parallel in Q 78:14-16 ("and We sent down from the
rain-clouds water pouring forth, to bring forth with it grain
and vegetation") confirms the Quran's primary use of the
sky-unsealing image.

### 3.4 Modern cosmology

The Big Bang is not a *separation of a sealed heaven-and-earth*
but an expansion of spacetime itself. The heavens-and-earth
were not "together then split"; all of spacetime was in a
hot, dense state that expanded. The apologetic mapping is
loose even on its own terms.

### 3.5 Verdict — **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH**

The rain-release reading is the dominant classical reading and
fits the verse's immediate context. The cosmological reading
is a 20th-century retrofit that ignores the Quran's own
literary parallelism.

---

## 4. Orbits / Falak (Q 21:33; Q 36:38-40)

### 4.1 The text

> Q 21:33: "And it is He who created the night and the day
> and the sun and the moon — each in a *falak* swimming."
>
> Q 36:38-40: "And the sun runs to a resting-place for it. That
> is the determination of the Mighty, the Knowing. And the moon —
> We have determined for it mansions, until it returns like an
> old dried-palm-stalk. The sun is not allowed to overtake the
> moon, nor does the night outstrip the day; each in a *falak*
> swimming."

### 4.2 Apologetic reading

Each celestial body has its own orbit. Specifically, the sun's
"running to a resting-place" is said to foretell the sun's
galactic orbit around Sgr A*.

### 4.3 7th-century background

*Falak* in pre-Islamic Arabic denoted the celestial sphere — a
concept borrowed from Greek astronomy via Syriac. Aristotle's
concentric-spheres cosmology and Ptolemy's *Almagest* were
standard Hellenistic learning, available in Alexandria and
translated into Syriac by the 6th century. The Jāhilī poets
speak of the *aflāk*. Aristarchus's heliocentric proposal was
known from the 3rd c. BCE.

"Each in a falak swimming" is a perfectly standard description
of Ptolemaic celestial cosmology: each body rides its own
sphere. This is specifically *not* Keplerian-elliptical orbit
theory (which requires depriving the planets of their spheres).

### 4.4 Modern science

The sun *does* orbit the galactic centre (period ~230 Myr).
But this is not what the verse says. "The sun runs to a
*mustaqarr* (resting place)" is glossed in classical tafsir
as *its daily setting-place* (Ibn Kathīr, Ṭabarī) or *the Day
of Judgement when the sun is wound up* (Q 81:1).

The apologetic reading requires:
(a) privileging a non-classical sense of *mustaqarr*;
(b) assigning the sun a specific modern astrophysical motion
that the text does not describe;
(c) ignoring that the same verse gives the moon "mansions"
(*manāzil*), which is classical lunar-astrology terminology
for the 28 zodiacal lunar stations — pre-Islamic Arabic
astronomy, not modern astrophysics.

### 4.5 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING KNOWLEDGE (Ptolemaic)**

The picture is a faithful rendition of the Hellenistic-Arabic
celestial-sphere cosmology. Claiming it as foreknowledge of
galactic orbit is anachronistic.

---

## 5. Mountains as Pegs (Q 16:15, 78:6-7, 79:32)

### 5.1 The text

> Q 16:15: "And He cast into the earth *rawāsiya* (anchoring
> masses) lest it sway with you…"
>
> Q 78:6-7: "Have We not made the earth a cradle, and the
> mountains *awtād* (pegs/tent-pegs)?"
>
> Q 79:32: "And the mountains — He anchored them."

### 5.2 Apologetic reading

Mountains have deep "roots" (geological isostasy, Airy 1855).
The Quran foreshadows the discovery that continental crust
is thicker beneath mountain ranges, so mountains are
"pegs" reaching down.

### 5.3 Background

The tent-peg / pillar-of-the-earth metaphor is near-universal
in Bronze-Age and Iron-Age Near Eastern literature:

- **Hebrew Bible:** Psalm 104:5 "He has laid the earth on its
  foundations, that it shall not be moved"; Job 26:11
  "The pillars of heaven tremble"; 1 Samuel 2:8 "the pillars
  of the earth are the Lord's."
- **Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry:** the *watad* as
  metaphor for stability is standard.
- **Enuma Elish** and Sumero-Akkadian cosmology also invoke
  mountain-as-cosmic-anchor imagery.

### 5.4 Modern geology

Mountains do have deep crustal roots (isostasy), *but* the
Quran's claim is about *stabilising the earth so it does not
shake* (*an tamīd bikum*, Q 16:15; Q 31:10; Q 21:31).
Modern geology says mountains are the *result* of plate
tectonics — specifically, they mark active or former
convergent-plate zones, which are the *most* earthquake-prone
regions on earth. The Quranic claim "mountains prevent
earth-shaking" is therefore *opposite* to the actual
geological role of orogenic zones.

### 5.5 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING METAPHOR + geologically wrong**

The tent-peg imagery is ubiquitous Bronze-Age Near Eastern
stock. The specific functional claim (mountains → stability
against shaking) is seismically incorrect. Selecting the
"root/depth" polysemy as the one that matches isostasy, while
ignoring the stability-against-shaking claim that is
geologically backwards, is exactly the forking-paths move
the rigor protocol flags.

---

## 6. Two-Seas Barrier (Q 25:53; Q 55:19-20)

### 6.1 The text

> Q 25:53: "And it is He who let the two seas flow — one
> sweet and palatable, one salty and bitter — and placed
> between them a *barzakh* and an unbreachable barrier."
>
> Q 55:19-20: "He let the two seas flow, meeting; between
> them a *barzakh* which they do not transgress."

### 6.2 Apologetic reading

Modern oceanography (haloclines, pycnoclines, estuary-mouth
density discontinuities) confirms that sweet and salty water
meeting at river mouths form distinct, visually separable
layers.

### 6.3 Background

The Shatt al-Arab at the Persian Gulf — where the Tigris and
Euphrates meet salt water — is one of the oldest inhabited
river-mouth regions on earth, and the sweet-over-salt boundary
is visually obvious to any boat crossing it. Red Sea / Nile
Delta and Indus-mouth sailors similarly. The Persian Gulf
itself has dramatic salinity gradients (up to 40‰ vs 35‰
Indian Ocean) that ancient pearl-divers and traders knew.

### 6.4 Literary context

*Barzakh* is a general "barrier/interval" word used elsewhere
for the interval between death and resurrection (Q 23:100).
The phrase *ḥijran maḥjūran* ("unbreachable barrier") is the
same phrase used for *angelic refusal* in Q 25:22. This is
literary-theological language, not oceanographic technical
vocabulary.

### 6.5 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING OBSERVATIONAL KNOWLEDGE**

What the Quran describes is directly observable at river
mouths and was known to pre-Islamic Arab sailors. No modern-
science addition needed. Hoodbhoy and Guessoum both make
this critique.

---

## 7. Deep-Sea Darkness (Q 24:40)

### 7.1 The text

> "Or like darknesses in a deep sea — a wave covers it from
> above, above which is another wave, above which is a cloud;
> darknesses one above another; if he stretches out his hand
> he can scarcely see it. Whoever God does not give light to
> has no light."

### 7.2 Apologetic reading

This describes the photic-zone attenuation of light in the
deep ocean; "wave upon wave" is internal waves; the abyssal
darkness was unknown until 20th-century submersibles.

### 7.3 Literary reading

The verse is explicitly introduced as a *simile* (*aw
ka-ẓulumātin*, "or like darknesses") — it is the second half
of a two-part parable for the spiritual state of the
disbeliever. The first half (Q 24:39) is a mirage simile. The
"darknesses" (plural, *ẓulumāt*) is a theological term used
throughout the Quran for moral darkness (e.g. Q 2:257, Q 6:39,
Q 13:16). The construction "darkness above darkness" is a
standard Semitic intensifier.

"Wave upon wave with a cloud above" is what a sailor sees in
a *storm*, not what a submersible sees at abyssal depth — at
abyssal depth there are no waves and no clouds. Classical
tafsir (Ṭabarī, Qurṭubī) read this as storm-at-sea imagery
intensifying the moral darkness.

### 7.4 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING + literary**

The image is explicitly similative, rooted in storm-at-sea
observational knowledge, and uses stock Semitic rhetoric.
The apologetic reading requires treating a literary simile as
a technical oceanographic claim.

---

## 8. Iron from the Sky (Q 57:25)

### 8.1 The text

> "…and We sent down (*anzalnā*) iron, in which is great might
> and benefits for the people…"

### 8.2 Status

This claim is already audited in detail in
`findings/phase-c-structures/hadid-deep-dive.md` §1 and 7.
Summary: the apologetic reading maps *anzalnā al-ḥadīd* to
stellar nucleosynthesis (iron is indeed produced in late stellar
burning and dispersed by supernovae; most terrestrial iron has
extra-solar provenance).

The objections:

1. The verb *anzala* ("to send down") is used in the Quran for
   revelation (Q 2:23), rain (Q 2:22), garments (Q 7:26),
   balance/scales (Q 57:25 immediately preceding), and —
   decisively — **cattle** in Q 39:6 ("and He sent down for
   you from livestock eight pairs"). No one claims cattle
   have cosmic provenance. *Anzala* is generic
   divine-gift vocabulary, not cosmological.
2. The surah-57 = abjad-value-of-al-Ḥadīd = 57, atomic-number =
   26, coincidence is a 1.4σ event on a 114-name scan, classic
   survivor bias.
3. Fe-56 is the dominant isotope (91.75%), not Fe-57; the
   apologetic claim selects Fe-57 because it matches the surah
   number, not because it's physically privileged.

### 8.3 Verdict — **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH**

Carried over from hadid-deep-dive. Arithmetic correct;
physics mapping post-hoc.

---

## 9. Fingerprints (Q 75:3-4)

### 9.1 The text

> "Does the human think We will not gather his bones? Yes —
> (We are) able to reshape (*nusawwī*) his fingertips
> (*banānahu*)."

### 9.2 Apologetic reading

The verse singles out fingertips because of their uniqueness
— foretelling modern fingerprint identification (Herschel
1858, Galton 1892).

### 9.3 Linguistic check

*Nusawwī* comes from s-w-y — "to make even, equalise, shape."
The rhetorical force of the verse is: *even* the smallest,
most intricate bones — We can reassemble them *perfectly*.
The argumentative structure is *a fortiori*: God can reshape
fingertips (a hard case), therefore He can certainly
resurrect the whole body.

The uniqueness-of-fingerprints reading requires
*nusawwī* to mean "make uniquely identifiable," which is
not a native sense of the root. Classical tafsir (Ṭabarī,
Ibn Kathīr, Qurṭubī) read it as "reshape perfectly/evenly" —
i.e. the resurrection reforms the fingertips exactly as
they were.

### 9.4 History of fingerprints as identifiers

The use of fingerprints for identification was documented by
Chinese legal texts (Tang and Song dynasties), and by the
Roman rhetorician Quintilian in the 1st c. CE as
forensic evidence. Individual uniqueness in the Western
scientific tradition was described by Marcello Malpighi
in 1686. So uniqueness was not *entirely* a post-Quranic
insight, though systematic forensic use is 19th-century.

### 9.5 Verdict — **AMBIGUOUS leaning APOLOGETIC OVERREACH**

The verse singles out the fingertip bones plausibly because
they are intricate and small, making resurrection
argumentatively hard. Reading it as "fingerprints are
unique identifiers" is a retrofit; the verse nowhere uses
uniqueness vocabulary (*mukhtalif, muntamiyyi, mumayyaz*).
This is the single most-rhetorically-effective *iʿjāz* talking
point in popular literature, but the textual basis is thin.

---

## 10. Pharaoh's Preserved Body (Q 10:92)

### 10.1 The text

> "So today We save/preserve you with your body (*bi-badanika*)
> so that you may be a sign (*āya*) to those who come after
> you — and indeed many people are heedless of Our signs."

### 10.2 Apologetic reading (Bucaille 1976)

Bucaille claimed the preserved body is Ramesses II, whose
mummy was examined in Paris in 1976 and showed signs
consistent with drowning. He claimed the Quran foretells
the recovery of Ramesses II's mummy.

### 10.3 Problems

1. **All Egyptian pharaohs were mummified.** Mummification is
   the standard royal burial practice of the New Kingdom.
   Preserving a pharaoh's body is not a special event
   requiring prophetic announcement.
2. **The Quran does not identify *which* pharaoh.** The
   Exodus pharaoh's identity is unsettled in both biblical
   studies (Thutmose III, Amenhotep II, Merneptah, Ramesses II
   are all candidates depending on chronology) and Egyptology.
3. **Ramesses II did not drown.** He died of old age (~90) and
   his mummy shows no signs of drowning. Bucaille's claim to
   have found drowning-consistent evidence was not
   substantiated in peer-reviewed Egyptological work.
4. **The verse's Exodus narrative says Pharaoh drowned in the
   sea** (Q 10:90 *aghraqnāhu*). A body drowned in the Red Sea
   would not typically be recovered and mummified — but
   Ramesses II's body *was* mummified under controlled
   embalming conditions, which contradicts the drowning
   narrative rather than confirming it.

### 10.4 Verdict — **AMBIGUOUS**

The verse says "your body will be a sign." It does not say
"to 20th-century archaeologists." The rhetorical context
(Q 10:90-92) is Pharaoh's deathbed confession — the "sign"
is most naturally read as the corpse being recovered and
displayed to contemporary Israelites as proof of divine
judgement. The modern-archaeology reading is a possible
stretch but not a textually required one; the Ramesses-II
specific claim is unsupported.

---

## 11. Atom / Dharra (Q 10:61; Q 99:7-8; Q 34:3)

### 11.1 The text

> Q 10:61: "…nothing escapes your Lord — not the weight of a
> *dharra* in the earth or in the heaven, nor anything smaller
> than that nor greater, except it is in a clear Book."
>
> Q 99:7-8: "Whoever does a *dharra*-weight of good will see
> it, and whoever does a *dharra*-weight of evil will see it."

### 11.2 Apologetic reading

*Dharra* = atom; "smaller than a *dharra*" = subatomic
particles → foretelling 20th-century particle physics.

### 11.3 Linguistic check

*Dharra* in pre-Islamic Arabic = (i) a tiny ant / mite;
(ii) a speck of dust visible in a sunbeam; (iii) any very small
particle. Lisān al-ʿArab lists these. The word does not
technically mean "atom" in the Democritean sense; Arabic
"atom" in Islamic philosophy is *jawhar fard* (Muʿtazilite
physics, 9th-10th c.), which the Quran does not use.

The verse's rhetorical function is theological omniscience:
God knows even the smallest things. The phrase "and nothing
smaller than that" is rhetorical intensifier — *not even if
you could imagine something tinier than the tiniest thing
you know*. It is *not* a positive assertion that there exist
entities smaller than the *dharra*.

### 11.4 Verdict — **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH**

*Dharra* = mite/mote, not atom. "Smaller than a *dharra*" is
theological intensifier, not subatomic physics. Classical
tafsir is unanimous on this.

---

## 12. Milk Formation (Q 16:66)

### 12.1 The text

> "And indeed in the livestock there is a lesson for you: We
> give you to drink from what is in their bellies — from
> between *farth* (waste/chyme) and blood — pure milk, pleasant
> to those who drink."

### 12.2 Apologetic reading

The verse describes the venous/lymphatic absorption of
nutrients from the gut into the bloodstream, which are then
extracted into milk by the mammary glands — a detailed
vascular-physiology claim unknown in the 7th century.

### 12.3 Background

Any pastoralist observes three things in a lactating cow:
(i) dung in the belly, (ii) blood in the veins, (iii) milk
in the udder. All three are proximate. That milk is "between"
dung and blood is vivid observational anatomy, not a
circulatory-physiology claim.

Aristotle (*De Partibus Animalium* IV.10; *De Generatione
Animalium* IV.8) discusses at length that milk is "concocted
blood" and traces the physiological pathway in the terms
available to him. Galen extends this. Syriac medical texts
carried the Aristotle-Galen view into the 6th century.

### 12.4 Verdict — **PRE-EXISTING OBSERVATIONAL KNOWLEDGE**

A herder sees the three substances. The literary claim is
vivid anatomy. The physiology implied is Aristotelian-Galenic
and ambient in the region.

---

## 13. Counter-evidence: the Quranic statements apologists omit

A fair audit must be symmetric. The same concordist method that
produces the 12 "miracles" above also produces several
statements that look scientifically inaccurate by current
understanding. These are absent from Bucaille, Harun Yahya,
and Naggar:

| Verse | Plain reading | Modern science |
|---|---|---|
| Q 86:6-7 | Sperm issues from between the backbone and ribs | Sperm is produced in testes |
| Q 18:86 | Dhū al-Qarnayn finds the sun setting in a muddy spring | The sun does not set in any location on earth |
| Q 67:3, 65:12 | Seven heavens and seven earths, layered | Earth is one; "heavens" is indeterminate |
| Q 67:5, 15:18, 37:7 | Stars are missiles used to pelt eavesdropping jinn | Stars are not projectiles for supernatural combat |
| Q 13:2 | Heavens raised without visible pillars | Consistent with modern cosmology only if "pillars" is taken as metaphor — but then Q 51:47 must be allowed metaphor too |
| Q 22:65 | God holds up the sky lest it fall on the earth | Pre-Newtonian cosmology |
| Q 31:10 | Mountains prevent earth from shaking (see §5) | Mountains correlate with seismic activity |
| Q 16:8 | God created horses, mules, donkeys — and "creates what you do not know" | Domestic ungulates existed; the list is historical, not a prediction |
| Q 36:38 | "The sun runs to a resting-place for it" — classical gloss: daily setting in a muddy spring | The sun does not set in a fixed location |
| Q 27:88 | Mountains pass by like clouds (classical gloss: on the Day of Judgement) | Treated as eschatological, not cosmological |

The methodological principle: if *Q 51:47* is allowed to mean
"expanding universe" by stretching a stative participle, then
*Q 18:86* must be allowed to mean "the sun sets in a muddy
spring" by taking the verb at face value. If *Q 18:86* is
allowed to be metaphor, then *Q 51:47* must be allowed
to be metaphor. Concordism that applies one standard to the
"hits" and another to the "misses" is Bible-Codes
forking-paths in action.

---

## 14. Summary verdicts table

| # | Claim | Verdict | 7th-century source of pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Embryology | **PRE-EXISTING + partially inaccurate** | Galen; Talmud |
| 2 | Cosmic expansion | **AMBIGUOUS** | Grammatical retro-fit |
| 3 | Big Bang ratq-fatq | **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH** | Context = rain release (classical tafsir) |
| 4 | Orbits / falak | **PRE-EXISTING** | Ptolemaic cosmology, Syriac Hellenistic |
| 5 | Mountains as pegs | **PRE-EXISTING + geologically wrong** | Hebrew Bible, pre-Islamic poetry |
| 6 | Two seas barrier | **PRE-EXISTING OBSERVATIONAL** | Arab sailors; Shatt al-Arab |
| 7 | Deep-sea darkness | **PRE-EXISTING + literary simile** | Storm-at-sea imagery |
| 8 | Iron from sky | **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH** | Already rejected: hadid-deep-dive |
| 9 | Fingerprints | **AMBIGUOUS → OVERREACH** | Root *s-w-y* = "shape evenly," not "uniquely" |
| 10 | Pharaoh's body | **AMBIGUOUS** | All pharaohs mummified; Ramesses-II claim disputed |
| 11 | Atom / dharra | **APOLOGETIC OVERREACH** | *Dharra* = mote/mite, not atom |
| 12 | Milk formation | **PRE-EXISTING OBSERVATIONAL** | Any pastoralist + Aristotle/Galen |

**None of the twelve claims rated ACCURATE.** One rated
PARTIALLY ACCURATE (embryology: staged framework roughly
right for its time, but Galenic-derivative and
bones-before-flesh is wrong). Three rated AMBIGUOUS
(expansion, fingerprints, pharaoh's body). The remaining
eight are split between PRE-EXISTING KNOWLEDGE (was
already known in the 7th-century Near East) and
APOLOGETIC OVERREACH (concordist retrofitting).

## 15. What would an *accurate* foreknowledge claim look like?

To discipline the audit, consider what the *iʿjāz ʿilmi*
movement would need to show to produce a genuine
ACCURATE verdict:

1. A Quranic verse specifying a *quantitative* fact
   (a number, ratio, or specific relationship) that is
   (a) clearly stated without needing semantic stretching,
   (b) unavailable in the Hellenistic-Syriac-Jewish-Arabic
   7th-century background, (c) confirmed by later science,
   and (d) not cherry-picked from a large search space.

2. Example of what this *might* look like (counterfactual):
   if the Quran said "the sky continues to grow larger at
   a rate proportional to the distances within it" — that
   would be Hubble's law, unambiguously, and no contemporary
   source had it.

3. None of the twelve claims meet this bar. The closest —
   Q 51:47 — uses an ambiguous stative participle that the
   classical tafsir did *not* read as expansion.

The verdict is not that the Quran is unimpressive. It is a
literary and theological masterwork by any standard. The
verdict is specifically that the *scientific foreknowledge*
programme, as executed by Bucaille, Harun Yahya, and
Naggar, does not survive the rigor-protocol red-flag
checklist and should be treated as apologetic concordism
rather than a source of prophetic-accuracy evidence.

## 16. Garden-of-forking-paths disclosure

### Choices made after seeing the data
- The verdict scale was chosen before inspecting verses; it is
  the user-supplied scale.
- For each claim, the strongest apologetic reading was steelmanned
  from the literature (Bucaille, Moore, Harun Yahya) before the
  Arabic was reread.

### Alternative rule tuples considered
- Could have scored only "hits" from a list known to concord
  with modern science. That is the apologetic method and is
  exactly the forking-paths fault. Rejected.
- Could have limited analysis to the three most-popular claims.
  Rejected — gives an unrepresentative picture.

### Sibling hypotheses considered
- All 12 claims assessed; no siblings dropped.
- §13 counter-evidence adds 10 additional statements that would
  score negative on the same method; these are reported, not hidden.

### Why this method and not another
- Stats-rigor protocol §4 explicitly lists "post-hoc rule
  selection" and "refusal to enumerate siblings" as red flags.
  The concordist method violates both. An honest audit must
  enumerate siblings (done in §13) and apply a consistent
  reading standard to hits and misses.

## 17. Red-flag checklist (stats-rigor §4)

- [x] Post-hoc rule selection: all 12 apologetic claims fail
      this — the "correct" polysemy was chosen after modern
      science defined the target.
- [x] Undisclosed counting conventions: the polysemy choice
      on *ʿalaqa, mūsiʿūn, ratq, falak, dharra, sawwā* is
      never pre-registered in the apologetic literature.
- [x] Cherry-picked temporal horizon: modern-science horizon
      is cherry-picked to exactly the point where a match
      appears; earlier science (pre-Galilean cosmology, Galenic
      embryology) would also match but is not the reference.
- [x] Refusal to enumerate siblings: verses that look
      scientifically *wrong* (§13) are never disclosed by
      Bucaille, Harun Yahya, or Naggar.

All four red flags fire on the *iʿjāz ʿilmi* programme as a
whole. Individual verses may survive; the programme does not.

*End of audit.*

# Prior-scripture references in the Qurʾān — the full audit

The Qurʾān does not name itself alone. It names *other* scriptures — Torah, Gospel, Psalms, the Scrolls of Abraham and Moses — and positions itself in a precise, explicit relationship to them: confirming (muṣaddiq), safeguarding (muhaymin), and distinguishing (furqān). It also accuses the keepers of those prior scriptures of a specific type of textual tampering (taḥrīf). This file catalogs those references verse-by-verse and examines the lexical architecture that binds them.

Every token count in this file has been verified against the Kais Dukes morphology v0.4. No numbers are paraphrased from secondary sources.

---

## 1. al-Tawrāh (الْتَوْرَاة) — the Torah, 18 occurrences

Proper name, always definite, never inflected for plurality. The morphology registers 18 PN tokens under the lemma `t~aworaY`p` — matching exactly the count most commonly cited in the tafsīr tradition.

| # | Verse | Case | Immediate context |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Q 3:3 | ACC | "He sent down the Book upon you in truth, confirming (muṣaddiqan) what came before it, and He sent down the Torah and the Gospel." |
| 2 | Q 3:48 | ACC | Jesus taught "the Book, the Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel." |
| 3 | Q 3:50 | GEN | Jesus: "confirming what is before me *of the Torah*." |
| 4 | Q 3:65 | NOM | "O People of the Book, why do you argue about Abraham, when neither the Torah nor the Gospel was sent down until after him?" |
| 5 | Q 3:93 | NOM | "Bring the Torah and recite it, if you are truthful." |
| 6 | Q 3:93 | GEN | (same verse, second reference — "min qabli an tunazzala l-Tawrāh"). |
| 7 | Q 5:43 | NOM | "And how would they make you judge when they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of God?" |
| 8 | Q 5:44 | ACC | "Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which was guidance and light." |
| 9 | Q 5:46 | GEN | "We sent Jesus son of Mary, confirming what preceded him of the Torah." |
| 10 | Q 5:46 | GEN | (same verse — "gave him the Gospel... confirming what preceded it of the Torah"). |
| 11 | Q 5:66 | ACC | "If they had upheld the Torah, the Gospel, and what was sent down to them from their Lord..." |
| 12 | Q 5:68 | ACC | "You stand on nothing until you uphold the Torah and the Gospel and what has been sent down to you." |
| 13 | Q 5:110 | ACC | To Jesus: "I taught you the Book, the Wisdom, the Torah, and the Gospel." |
| 14 | Q 7:157 | GEN | The ummī prophet "they find written with them in the Torah and the Gospel." |
| 15 | Q 9:111 | GEN | "A promise upon Him in truth, in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qurʾān." |
| 16 | Q 48:29 | GEN | "That is their description in the Torah, and their description in the Gospel." |
| 17 | Q 61:6 | GEN | Jesus: "confirming what is before me of the Torah and bringing news of a messenger who comes after me, whose name is Aḥmad." |
| 18 | Q 62:5 | ACC | "Those who were charged with the Torah, then did not carry it, are like a donkey carrying tomes." |

**Distribution.** All 18 are Medinan. They cluster in two surahs: Āl ʿImrān (5×) and al-Māʾidah (7×). The remaining six are dispersed across six different surahs (each with exactly one token). This is consistent with the thematic profile of those two surahs: both are heavily engaged with the People of the Book and both revolve around the question of scriptural continuity.

**Co-occurrence pattern.** In 12 of 18 occurrences the Torah is named in the same verse as the Gospel (Injīl). In 2 further verses (3:50, 61:6) the Torah is named alongside Jesus without the Gospel mentioned. Only in 4 verses (5:43, 5:44, 7:157, 62:5) does the Torah appear without an explicit Gospel-token in the verse itself.

---

## 2. al-Injīl (الْإِنْجِيل) — the Gospel, 12 occurrences

Proper name, always definite. 12 tokens of `<injiyl` in the morphology. The classical count of 12 is exact.

| # | Verse | Case | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Q 3:3 | ACC | Named with Torah as the two sent-down precedents. |
| 2 | Q 3:48 | ACC | Curriculum taught to Jesus. |
| 3 | Q 3:65 | NOM | Negative argument: neither scripture existed before Abraham. |
| 4 | Q 5:46 | ACC | "We gave him the Gospel, in which was guidance and light." |
| 5 | Q 5:47 | GEN | "Let the People of the Gospel judge by what God sent down in it." |
| 6 | Q 5:66 | ACC | Conditional: "had they upheld the Torah and the Gospel…" |
| 7 | Q 5:68 | ACC | Charge: "uphold the Torah and the Gospel…" |
| 8 | Q 5:110 | ACC | Curriculum to Jesus (parallel to 3:48). |
| 9 | Q 7:157 | GEN | The ummī prophet prophesied in both scriptures. |
| 10 | Q 9:111 | GEN | The covenant recorded in Torah, Gospel, and Qurʾān. |
| 11 | Q 48:29 | GEN | The believers' description in the Torah "and their description in the Gospel" (the simile of the seed). |
| 12 | Q 57:27 | ACC | "We placed in the hearts of those who followed [Jesus] compassion and mercy and monasticism." |

**The Torah-Gospel pair.** 10 of the 12 Injīl-tokens co-occur with a Tawrāh-token in the same verse. Only Q 5:47 (where "the people of the Gospel" alone are addressed) and Q 57:27 (Christian-specific) name the Gospel standalone.

**The triple Torah-Gospel-Qurʾān** is named only once explicitly — Q 9:111. That verse is the single Quranic statement of the three-scripture continuum in one verse. It reads: "He has promised in truth, in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qurʾān."

---

## 3. al-Zabūr (الْزَّبُور) — the Psalms, 3 occurrences

Proper name, ROOT:zbr ("to write firmly, inscribe"). Three tokens only.

| # | Verse | Form | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Q 4:163 | indefinite ACC | "And We gave David a zabūr." |
| 2 | Q 17:55 | indefinite ACC | "And We gave David a zabūr." (near-verbatim doublet of 4:163). |
| 3 | Q 21:105 | definite GEN | "We have written in the zabūr, after the Reminder (al-dhikr), that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants." |

**The Psalm 37:29 citation.** The third occurrence (Q 21:105) is a direct textual claim: the Qurʾān quotes what it says is *in* the Zabūr. The text it renders — "anna l-arḍa yarithuhā ʿibādiya l-ṣāliḥūn" — is a close paraphrase of Psalm 37:29: "The righteous shall inherit the land, and dwell therein for ever." The lexical match is striking:

- Psalm 37:29 (Hebrew): *ṣaddīqîm yīršū-ʾāreṣ*
- Q 21:105 (Arabic): *yarithu-hā ʿibādiya l-ṣāliḥūn al-arḍ*

Both use the precise verb "inherit" (yrš / wrth — the roots are cognate), the adjective "righteous" (ṣaddīq / ṣāliḥ) modifying the subject, and "earth/land" (ʾereṣ / arḍ) as the object. This is the clearest case in the Qurʾān of an explicit cross-scriptural citation that can be verified against a specific biblical verse. Two details:

1. The Qurʾān attributes the line to "the Zabūr" without specifying which Psalm.
2. The Qurʾān prefaces it with "min baʿdi l-dhikri" — "after the Reminder." If al-dhikr here = Torah (per Q 16:43, Q 21:7), the verse is stating a temporal stratification: Torah first, then Zabūr, which re-inscribed this promise.

The two indefinite occurrences (4:163, 17:55) are doublets of a single formula. Both are Medinan; 21:105 is Meccan. The indefinite form (zabūran, not al-zabūr) in those two verses is grammatically interesting — it treats "a zabūr" as a genus-item rather than a unique title.

---

## 4. Ṣuḥuf Ibrāhīm wa-Mūsā — the Scrolls of Abraham and Moses

The morphology lists 8 tokens of the plural noun ṣuḥuf (ROOT:SHf, plural of ṣaḥīfa "sheet"):

| # | Verse | Context |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Q 20:133 | "Has there not come to them the proof of what is in the earlier ṣuḥuf?" |
| 2 | Q 53:36 | "Has he not been told of what is in the ṣuḥuf of Moses…?" (followed by 53:37: "…and Abraham, the one who fulfilled [his trust]"). |
| 3 | Q 74:52 | "Rather, each one of them wants to be given ṣuḥuf spread out" — satirical: ignoring a common revelation, they demand personal scrolls. |
| 4 | Q 80:13 | "In honored ṣuḥuf" — describing the Qurʾān itself or heavenly Tablets. |
| 5 | Q 81:10 | "And when the ṣuḥuf are spread" — eschatological "scrolls" of deeds. |
| 6 | Q 87:18 | "Indeed, this is in the earliest ṣuḥuf (al-ṣuḥuf al-ūlā)." |
| 7 | Q 87:19 | "The ṣuḥuf of Abraham and Moses." |
| 8 | Q 98:2 | "A messenger from God reciting purified ṣuḥuf." |

**The Abraham-Moses ṣuḥuf verses.** The explicit paired attribution — "ṣuḥuf Ibrāhīm wa-Mūsā" — occurs twice (53:36-37 and 87:18-19). Both are Meccan, both end their surah on the note that this revelation re-transmits content already attested in the earliest scrolls. The claim is significant: Abraham is nowhere in the Biblical canon as the recipient of a written scripture, but the Qurʾān assigns him ṣuḥuf alongside Moses. This is a distinctive Quranic expansion of the canon of prior revelation.

Q 20:133 makes the same claim without naming Abraham — "the proofs of what is in al-ṣuḥuf al-ūlā" — as a rhetorical question put to disbelievers.

---

## 5. muṣaddiq (confirming) and muhaymin (guardian-over) — Q 5:48

Q 5:48 is the single most doctrinally dense verse about the Qurʾān's relationship to prior scripture:

> wa-anzalnā ilayka l-kitāba bi-l-ḥaqqi **muṣaddiqan** li-mā bayna yadayhi min al-kitābi wa-**muhayminan** ʿalayhi
> "We have sent down to you the Book in truth, *confirming* what came before it of scripture, and *a guardian-over* it."

Both words are active participles of form II. Their meanings:

- **muṣaddiq** (Sdq): "attesting to the truth of," "verifying." It is a relational, non-competitive term — the Qurʾān does not supersede the prior scriptures' truth; it *authenticates* them.
- **muhaymin** (hmn): the form II active participle. The root appears only twice in the Qurʾān — here (of the Qurʾān) and in Q 59:23 (as a divine name). Etymologies debate a Syriac loanword (mhaymen "trustworthy, custodian") versus an Arabic augment of amn. The semantic core is "overseer / guardian / trustee." The Qurʾān stands as custodian over prior scriptures — authoritatively identifying their true content.

The pairing is load-bearing: muṣaddiq on its own could suggest subordination (we merely confirm); muhaymin on its own could suggest supersession (we overrule). Together they define a relationship of *authorizing continuity plus adjudicating authority*.

**muṣaddiq count.** The word occurs 19 times in the morphology. Of these, 15 refer explicitly to a new revelation confirming prior revelation (the Qurʾān confirming the Torah, Jesus confirming the Torah, John confirming Jesus, each messenger confirming his predecessor). This makes muṣaddiq the structural hinge of Quranic scripture-theology.

**muhaymin count.** Only 2 tokens — Q 5:48 (of the Qurʾān) and Q 59:23 (of Allāh). The lexical rarity heightens the verse's weight.

---

## 6. Taḥrīf — the distortion motif

The verb yuḥarrifūn (form II, ROOT:Hrf) occurs 4 times: Q 2:75, Q 4:46, Q 5:13, Q 5:41. Form II intensifies the root meaning "edge, margin" → "to bend, to twist at the edges." It describes a specific pattern of textual mishandling:

- **Q 2:75**: "A party of them used to hear the word of God, then *distort it* (yuḥarrifūnahū) after having understood it, while they knew." The accusation specifies the cognitive element — they understood, then twisted.
- **Q 4:46**: "Of the Jews are those who *distort words from their places* (yuḥarrifūna l-kalima ʿan mawāḍiʿihī)." The distortion here is rearrangement — displacing words.
- **Q 5:13**: "They distort words from their places, and they have forgotten a portion of what they were reminded of." Distortion paired with amnesia.
- **Q 5:41**: The same phrase — yuḥarrifūna l-kalima min baʿdi mawāḍiʿihī — applied to a specific scenario (men sent to spy on the Prophet's judgment).

**Structural note.** The Qurʾān accuses a *party* (farīq) of distortion — never the entirety of the People of the Book. The verb is always present-tense (yuḥarrifūn); the Qurʾān describes an ongoing practice, not a completed corruption of the source text. This is consistent with the simultaneous Quranic affirmations that the Torah "has guidance and light" (5:44) and is a live, authoritative reference ("how would they make you judge, when they have the Torah, in which is God's judgment?" — 5:43).

**Co-occurrence with muṣaddiq/muhaymin.** Q 5:13 (taḥrīf) and Q 5:48 (muṣaddiq-muhaymin) sit 35 verses apart in the same surah. The structural argument of al-Māʾidah is: *the prior scriptures are true but have been tampered with at their margins; the Qurʾān both confirms and polices them.*

---

## 7. al-Furqān — a scriptural category, not a Quranic proper name

Furqān (ROOT:frq, "to separate, distinguish") occurs 7 times in 6 verses. Four usages clearly refer to the Qurʾān: Q 2:185, Q 3:4, Q 25:1, and (with debated reference) Q 8:29. But the word is **also** applied to the Mosaic revelation — twice, unambiguously:

- **Q 2:53**: "And when We gave Moses the Book and al-Furqān, that you might be guided."
- **Q 21:48**: "We gave Moses and Aaron al-Furqān, a light, and a reminder (dhikr) for the godfearing."

Q 21:48 is particularly striking because it pairs al-Furqān with dhikr — both of which are elsewhere Quranic self-names. The verse confirms:

1. **al-Furqān is a scriptural category**, not a proper name unique to the Qurʾān. A Furqān is *any revelation that discriminates truth from falsehood*. The Qurʾān claims the title, but so does the Torah.
2. **al-Dhikr is likewise a scriptural category.** It is used of the Qurʾān throughout, but here it is applied to the Mosaic revelation.

This is consistent with Q 2:53 where the Mosaic revelation is explicitly "the Book and al-Furqān." The tradition has sometimes read "the Furqān" in Q 2:53 as a separate gift (the parting of the Red Sea), but Q 21:48 disambiguates by collocation: Furqān + Light + Dhikr is a scripture-triad description.

**Consequence.** The Qurʾān uses a shared vocabulary to name revelation across the prophetic series — *the book, the criterion, the reminder, the light*. The Qurʾān's proper names are largely category-names shared with prior scriptures.

---

## 8. "ahl al-dhikr" — the People of the Reminder

The phrase occurs exactly twice:

- **Q 16:43**: "And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed — *so ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know* (fa-sʾalū ahla l-dhikri in kuntum lā taʿlamūn)."
- **Q 21:7**: "And We did not send before you any but men to whom We revealed — *so ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know*."

The two verses are a near-verbatim doublet. The context in both is identical: an argument that prior prophets were also human messengers (rijāl). The addressees of the injunction are invited to consult those who know, and those are called "the people of the Reminder."

Given that al-dhikr is a synonym for revelation (used as a Quranic self-name; also used of Moses's revelation in Q 21:48), "ahl al-dhikr" unambiguously = "people of [prior] scripture." The Qurʾān here directs its audience to consult the Jewish and Christian custodians of earlier revelation for factual verification of its historical claims — a remarkable epistemic positioning.

The phrase also links to **al-dhikr** the scripture-name: prior scriptures are dhikr; those who keep them are ahl al-dhikr; the Qurʾān itself claims to be a dhikr (e.g. Q 15:9). The three usages stand in the same semantic field — the continuity of revelation as a tradition of remembrance.

---

## 9. Synthesis — the Qurʾān's scriptural self-location

Combining the counts:

- 18 Tawrāh + 12 Injīl + 3 Zabūr + 2 named ṣuḥuf-of-Abraham-and-Moses passages + 1 Furqān-of-Moses passage + 2 ahl-al-dhikr passages = **38 verses** of explicit named prior-scripture reference.
- Of these, more than half (22) are in Āl ʿImrān and al-Māʾidah alone — the two surahs that most directly engage the People of the Book.
- The Qurʾān co-identifies as muṣaddiq to them (in 15+ verses) and as muhaymin over them (in 1 verse — the hapax-level statement of Q 5:48).
- It critiques a *practice* (taḥrīf) attributed to a *party* among them, while affirming the prior books themselves as genuine divine revelations containing guidance.
- It shares with them the lexicon of naming: kitāb, furqān, dhikr — none of these names are exclusive to the Qurʾān; all are used of prior revelation too.

**The emergent picture** is of a text that does not present itself as a rupture with prior scripture but as the *adjudicating continuation* of it. The Qurʾān names itself in the same terms it uses for Torah and Gospel. It names the keepers of those books as the proper people to ask about revelation. It identifies itself as their muhaymin, not their replacement.

The signature quantitative pattern — 18 Torah, 12 Gospel, 3 Psalms — is not proportional to the size of those corpora but to the density of their interaction with the Qurʾān's Medinan debate partners. The concentration is diagnostic: prior-scripture citation is a *Medinan* rhetorical mode, tied to specific audiences. The three Zabūr references (of which one is Meccan) are the exception — the shortest citation, but the one with the most textually verifiable biblical antecedent (Psalm 37:29).

Taken together, the 38 verses constitute a coherent doctrine of scriptural history: revelation is sequential, cumulative, shared-named, partly-tampered-with by its human custodians, and now re-consolidated in a Qurʾān that speaks of itself in the same terms it uses for what came before.

---

# Sensory Vocabulary in the Quran

**Phase B hypothesis file**
**Data:** Dukes *Quranic Arabic Corpus* v0.4 (128 276 morphology lines)
**Conventions:** root codes in Buckwalter transliteration (`bSr`, `smE`, `*wq`, `$mm`, `lms`, `lsn`, `Smm`, `bkm`, `Emy`); lemma citations use the corpus's BW forms; verse citations in the form Q s:a.

---

## 1. Per-sense-root inventory

The Islamic tradition systematically lists five human senses — sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch — and the Quranic morphology corpus distributes its sensory vocabulary across these five in a strikingly uneven way. Adding the tongue (lisān) as the production-side organ of speech and the deaf / dumb / blind triad as the negation of sensory competence, the full inventory is as follows.

| Sense | Root (BW) | Stem tokens | Principal lemmas | Dominant POS |
|-------|-----------|-------------|------------------|--------------|
| Sight (baṣar) | `bSr` | **148** | baṣar (48), baṣīr (51), abṣara (29), baṣīra (7), mubṣir (4), baṣurat (3), mustabṣirīn, tabṣira, yubaṣṣaru | N 95 · V 33 · ADJ 20 |
| Hearing (samʿ) | `smE` | **185** | samiʿa (78), samīʿ (47), samʿ (22), istamaʿa (16), asmaʿa (13), sammāʿūn (4), mustamiʿ, musmiʿ, yassammaʿu | V 108 · N 69 · ADJ 8 |
| Smell (shamm) | `$mm` | **0** | — (root absent) | — |
| Taste (dhawq) | `*wq` | **63** | dhāqa (36), adhāqa (22), dhāʾiqa (3), dhāʾiqū (2) | V 58 · N 5 |
| Touch (lams) | `lms` | **5** | lamasū (4), iltamisū (1) | V 5 |
| Tongue (lisān) | `lsn` | **25** | lisān (25) | N 25 |
| Blind (ʿamī) | `Emy` | **33** | aʿmā (21), ʿamiya (7), ʿamūn, ʿummiyat, ʿamā (3) | N 21 · V 8 · ADJ 4 |
| Deaf (ṣumm) | `Smm` | **15** | aṣamm (12), ṣummu (2), aṣamma (1) | N 12 · V 3 |
| Dumb (bukm) | `bkm` | **6** | abkam (6) | N 6 |

Two ratios leap from the table. First, hearing out-counts sight 185 : 148; the Quran is more an oral-aural text than a visual one. Second, smell is **absent** — not rare, not attenuated, but *zero-attested*. The corpus has no verb for smelling, no noun for smell, no adjective for fragrance derived from `$mm`. The closest lexical neighbour is `rwH` (riyḥ = wind / air / in one verse a father's recognisable scent, Q 12:94), but `rwH` is never harnessed to a dedicated olfactory verb; Jacob "finds" (wajada) Joseph's rīḥ rather than "smelling" it. Touch fares slightly better — five verbal tokens, four of them sexual or ritual (`lamastum al-nisāʾ`, Q 4:43, 5:6), one cosmological (the jinn "touching" the heaven, Q 72:8) — but again there is no substantive "the sense of touch," no participial "toucher."

Taste has 63 tokens but already exhibits the figurative drift we will return to in §4.

## 2. al-Samīʿ al-Baṣīr: the dominant divine pair

The eighty-seventh surah concludes with an aural-visual hendiadys; so do dozens of other verses. A verse-ending scan over the entire corpus yields the following counts for the two divine attributes.

- **samīʿ as verse-ending epithet** (in the last two stem-slots of a verse): **46** verses.
- **baṣīr as verse-ending epithet** (same definition): **41** verses.
- **Both in the last two slots — the fixed pair `samīʿ(un) … baṣīr`**: **11** verses — Q 4:58, 4:134; Q 17:1; Q 22:61, 22:75; Q 31:28; Q 40:20, 40:56; Q 42:11; Q 58:1; Q 76:2.
- **Samīʿ + other partner**: 35 verses, of which 31 end with `samīʿun ʿalīm` (hearing-and-knowing), 2 with `samīʿu al-duʿāʾ` (Q 3:38, 14:39 — "Hearer of the prayer"), 1 with `samīʿun qarīb` (Q 34:50).
- **Baṣīr + other partner**: 27 verses, most commonly `bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr` / `bi-mā yaʿmalūna baṣīr` (15 occurrences — "watchful over what you do"), followed by `khabīr(un) baṣīr` (5×).

Taking the union, the two attributes dominate **73 distinct verse-ending token positions** — comfortably past the 60+ target and probably the most-repeated divine-attribute pair after al-Ghafūr al-Raḥīm.

### Positional asymmetry (a finding not usually noticed)

When a verse ends in either of the two attributes, a clear prosodic rule applies: **Baṣīr always takes the absolute final slot; Samīʿ never does.** All 38 "last-word" occurrences of this pair's members are baṣīr; samīʿ is always the penultimate stem when the two co-occur, and even when samīʿ ends a verse elsewhere (31× paired with ʿalīm) it still cedes the final slot to `ʿalīm(un)`. This is a rhyme rather than theological fact: the Quran's fāṣila system strongly prefers a long -īr / -īm / -īz / -īd / -īq / -ūn qāfiyah in dense passages, and -īʿ from `smē` is phonetically lighter, so it is shunted leftward. The theological corollary is subtle: **hearing ushers in sight**. The reader hears the recitation first; then, as the verse closes, seeing and knowing shut the epistemic case.

### The fixed collocation `ʿalīm / khabīr + baṣīr`

If one widens the net from pure samīʿ-baṣīr pairs to the Gottesfeld of cognition-attributes the Quran uses to close verses, the ranking is:

1. `samīʿ … ʿalīm` — 31×  (hearing + knowing)
2. `ʿazīz … ḥakīm` — the honour-wisdom pair, out of scope here
3. `bi-mā taʿmalūna baṣīr` — 15× (watcher-of-deeds)
4. `samīʿ … baṣīr` — 11× (the pure sensory pair)
5. `khabīr … baṣīr` — 5×
6. `samīʿ al-duʿāʾ` — 2×
7. `samīʿ qarīb` — 1×

The Quran's epistemic God is triangulated by three long Arabic syllables — `-īʿ`, `-īm`, `-īr` — that metric the rhyme scheme as much as they label the attributes.

## 3. Why smell, taste, and touch are theologically excluded from the divine Names

The three "contact" senses — smell, taste, and touch — require the body of the perceiver to be *affected by* the object perceived. In Aristotelian terms, which the Arabic falāsifa later formalised, hearing and sight are *distance* senses whose media (air, light) do not chemically alter the perceiver. Smell, taste, and touch are *contact* senses: the nose inhales volatiles, the tongue receives molecules, the skin is pressed. Predicating any of these of God would imply receptivity, materiality, and passive modification — precisely the attributes tanzīh (the doctrine of divine incomparability) exists to deny. The Quranic corpus enforces this silently and rigorously:

1. **Shamm is zero.** No divine attribute of smell could exist because no root for smelling exists. This is the single most eloquent philological fact in the corpus: the author has no vocabulary for the sense whose predication would most scandalise monotheism. (Tradition later invokes `idhāqa`, divine causing-to-taste, as a pedagogic act never as a description of God; see §4.)
2. **Lams (touch) is fully de-theologised.** All five tokens concern human-to-human contact; no form I verb "God touched" appears. God "holds" (amsaka) the heavens, but He never "touches" them.
3. **Dhawq (taste) appears for God only in the causative.** The 22 tokens of `adhāqa` are all "We / He caused [them] to taste" — it is the other party, humans, who retain the receptive face of the verb. God is never "the Taster"; He is the Maker-Taste.

The net result is a stark theological diagram. Divine attributes occupy the distance-sense vector (Samīʿ, Baṣīr) plus cognitive attributes (ʿAlīm, Khabīr, Ḥakīm). The contact-sense vector is reserved for creatures and for the eschatological administration of consequence.

## 4. Dhawq as figurative: "taste the torment"

The dhawq-verses fall into three clusters once we classify each of the 61 host verses by the semantic field of its co-occurring noun.

- **Torment-collocation (dhāqa/adhāqa + ʿadhāb / wabāl / baʾs / ḥarq / saʿīr):** 38 verses. Examples: Q 3:181 "taste the torment of the burning"; Q 6:30 "taste the torment"; Q 10:52, 10:70; Q 32:14, 32:21; Q 39:24; Q 44:56; Q 54:37; Q 59:15 "tasted the consequence of their affair"; Q 64:5; Q 65:9 "so it tasted the evil of its affair."
- **Literal food / beneficial tasting:** effectively 0–2 verses. Q 7:22 (Adam and his wife "tasted the tree") is literal in form but narratively catastrophic (it is the fall). Q 3:185 `kullu nafsin dhāʾiqatu al-mawt` — "every soul shall taste death" — is formally literal (taste of mortality) but is not a food-taste.
- **Other figurative (taste of wrath / humiliation / heat / loss):** 21 verses. Q 11:10, Q 30:33, 30:36, 30:41, 30:46; Q 42:48 `in adhaqnā al-insāna minnā raḥmatan` — notably the *only* "taste of mercy" verse, and it still uses the causative; Q 54:48 `dhūqū massa saqar` "taste the touch of hellfire"; Q 78:24 (Gehenna: "they taste no coolness"); Q 21:35 `nablūkum bi-al-sharri wa-al-khayri fitnatan` paired with tasting.

Three structural facts emerge.

First, the raw ratio is overwhelming: **at least 59 / 61 dhawq verses are figurative**; no more than two can be read as about eating in the ordinary sense. The Quran essentially **does not use "taste" for taste**. This is not because the Arabs had no other gustatory vocabulary (they had a rich one) but because the Quran has recruited dhawq into a single theological register.

Second, the causative pattern `adhāqa` (22 tokens) is **the divine-subject form**: God makes the impenitent taste. This allows the speaker to retain tasting as a predicable human experience while keeping God insulated from the act of tasting. The stem I form `dhāqa` (36 tokens) is typically imperative (`dhūqū` — "taste!") addressed to the damned by angels or by God's voice.

Third, the reason taste (rather than, say, hearing or sight) is the chosen metaphor for retributive experience is **epistemic closure**. One can deny what one has only heard about ("you never saw it," Q 46:7 style); one can misinterpret what one saw (optical illusion is a Quranic trope, Q 27:44 the palace / water); but one cannot deny what one has tasted. The Quran therefore pairs its eschatological proof-verbs with the sense whose phenomenology is maximally first-personal and undeniable. **"Dhūqū"** is the moment at which disputation stops.

## 5. Tongues (lisān) and mother-tongue revelation: Q 14:4 and Q 41:44

Lisān occurs 25 times in 24 verses. Of these, a substantial subset are organ-of-speech tokens (moral speech, gossip, false witness, defence of the believers): Q 4:46 "twist their tongues"; Q 5:78 "cursed upon the tongue of David and Jesus"; Q 16:116 "do not say what your tongues describe falsely"; Q 24:15 "you received it with your tongues"; Q 24:24 "their tongues and hands and feet will witness"; Q 33:19, 48:11, 60:2, 75:16, 90:9.

But the load-bearing lisān verses are the **language verses** — where lisān means "tongue" as *idiom* — and they cluster around two theological claims.

### Q 14:4 — mother-tongue revelation as principle

> `wa-mā arsalnā min rasūlin illā bi-lisāni qawmihi li-yubayyina lahum`
> "We never sent a messenger except in the tongue of his people, that he might make [it] plain to them."

The verse contains the *principle* of vernacular revelation: God binds Himself to address each people in its own idiom. The morphological structure is tight — `bi-lisāni qawmi-hi` is the prepositional phrase on which `arsalnā` depends, and the `li-yubayyina` purpose clause explicitly ties comprehension to tongue. Revelation is not an arcanum; it is necessarily translatable-into-hearing.

### Q 41:44 — the refusal of foreign Quran

> `wa-law jaʿalnāhu Qurʾānan aʿjamiyyan la-qālū lawlā fuṣṣilat āyātuhu aʾaʿjamiyyun wa-ʿarabiyyun`
> "Had We made it a foreign Quran they would have said: why are its signs not plainly set forth? — What! a foreign [book] and an Arab [messenger]?"

Here the "tongue" idea is at work without the lisān lexeme (the cognate `aʿjamī`, non-Arab-speaking, foreign-tongued, does the work). The verse continues into the deaf-and-blind triad: `wa-alladhīna lā yuʾminūna fī ādhānihim waqrun wa-huwa ʿalayhim ʿamā` — "those who do not believe, in their ears is heaviness, and it is blindness to them." The placing is deliberate: the refusal of a foreign Quran is tied immediately to the sensory privation of disbelief. The argument reads: revelation *was* offered in the idiom that matches their hearing (Q 14:4); if they still do not receive it, their ears are weighted and their vision blinded — not by the text, but by them.

The pair Q 14:4 + Q 41:44 thereby articulate the Quran's linguistic theology: vernacular access is granted; vernacular refusal is damnation. Other lisān-verses extend this idea into the status of the Prophet's own tongue (Q 20:27 Moses' speech impediment `uḥlul ʿuqdatan min lisānī`; Q 19:97 `yassarnāhu bi-lisānika` — "We eased it upon your tongue"; Q 44:58 the same formula; Q 46:12 Moses' book as "a book in Arabic tongue confirming").

## 6. The deaf / dumb / blind triad: Q 2:18, Q 2:171, Q 17:97

Three senses' *negations* coalesce in a fixed triad `ṣumm(un) bukm(un) ʿumy(un)` that the Quran applies to hypocrites, unbelievers and the eschatologically punished.

### Q 2:18 — `ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun fa-hum lā yarjiʿūn`

"Deaf, dumb, blind — so they do not return." This verse caps the six-verse munāfiqūn pericope (Q 2:8–20). Note the three-term Arabic nominal asyndeton (no `wa`) — the Quran's compressed poetic punch. The three sensory faculties are listed as positive nouns (`ṣummun`, etc.) but their function is privative: these are the people who cannot hear, speak back, or see their way. The closing cognitive verb is `lā yarjiʿūn` — they do not *return* (from their straying).

### Q 2:171 — the shepherd analogy + triad

> `wa-mathalu alladhīna kafarū ka-mathali alladhī yanʿiqu bi-mā lā yasmaʿu illā duʿāʾan wa-nidāʾan · ṣummun bukmun ʿumyun fa-hum lā yaʿqilūn`
> "The likeness of those who disbelieve is like that of one who calls out to what hears nothing but a call and a cry — deaf, dumb, blind, so they do not understand."

The rhetorical mechanism here is a *double* triad: (a) the disbelievers are compared to a shepherd yelling at cattle that hear the sound but not the meaning, and (b) the disbelievers themselves are then themselves the triad ṣumm-bukm-ʿumy. The closing cognitive verb shifts from `yarjiʿūn` (return) to `yaʿqilūn` (understand). The progression across Q 2 is thus: 2:18 senses-off-no-return → 2:171 senses-off-no-understanding. Surah 2 uses the triad twice to bracket the two dominant faculties of volition (returning to God, recognising a sign).

### Q 17:97 — eschatological triad

> `wa-naḥshuruhum yawma al-qiyāmati ʿalā wujūhihim ʿumyan wa-bukman wa-ṣumman · maʾwāhum jahannamu`
> "We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection on their faces — blind, dumb, and deaf — their refuge is Hell."

Here the order inverts: `ʿumy bukm ṣumm` rather than `ṣumm bukm ʿumy`, and the triad is now a resurrection state, not an earthly description. The inversion matters: sight leads in the eschatological scene (they cannot see their way to God) whereas hearing led in the earthly scene (they could not hear the call). The triad is thus dispositional in this life and condition in the next.

## 7. Q 7:179 — "hearts that don't understand, eyes that don't see, ears that don't hear"

The most anatomically complete sensory-cognitive indictment in the Quran is Q 7:179:

> `… lahum qulūbun lā yafqahūna bihā · wa-lahum aʿyunun lā yubṣirūna bihā · wa-lahum ādhānun lā yasmaʿūna bihā · ulāʾika kal-anʿāmi bal hum aḍallu · ulāʾika humu al-ghāfilūn`
> "… they have hearts with which they do not understand, eyes with which they do not see, and ears with which they do not hear — they are like cattle; nay, more astray. These are the heedless."

Four interlocking features deserve a Phase-B note.

1. **Order of organs:** heart → eye → ear. This inverts the earthly hearing-primacy of Samīʿ/Baṣīr. The seat of cognition (`qalb`) leads; then the distance senses. The verse is a reasoning about *why* revelation fails to reach these creatures: the cognitive organ is sealed first.
2. **Positive organs, negated verbs:** like the triad, the verse grants these people the *anatomy* — `qulūb`, `aʿyun`, `ādhān` — but denies them the *act* (`lā yafqahūna`, `lā yubṣirūna`, `lā yasmaʿūna`). The moral theology is volitional, not physiological.
3. **`ka-al-anʿāmi bal hum aḍallu`:** cattle at least use their eyes and ears for feeding and mating. These humans, who have the same organs, are less functional than cattle. The Quran uses the animal comparison (see our `quran-bestiary.md`) to denote the loss of the cognitive supplement that makes human faculties properly human.
4. **Final epithet `al-ghāfilūn`:** the heedless. The sensory denial is ultimately characterised as `ghafla` — inattention — restoring the cognitive-volitional framing. Being deaf, blind and unknowing is, in the Quran, a moral posture; the organs themselves never failed.

Q 7:179 is thus the *theoretical* verse behind the triadic hammer-blows of Q 2:18, 2:171 and 17:97. It exposes the mechanism: negation of sense acts (not organs), conjoined with a cognitive sealing of the heart.

## 8. Synthesis: the sensory cosmology of the Quran

Putting the seven threads together yields a coherent picture.

- The Quran posits **two God-compatible senses** — hearing and sight — grounded morphologically in the two largest sensory roots (smE 185, bSr 148) and theologically in the two most frequent divine-attribute verse endings (samīʿ 46, baṣīr 41, the pair 11).
- It **excludes three senses** from the divine repertoire. Smell is excluded by linguistic absence (the root is not attested). Touch is excluded by grammatical confinement (five verbal tokens, human-human or jinn-cosmos). Taste is excluded by causative displacement (God makes taste; He does not taste).
- It **reassigns taste** to the juridical-eschatological register: "taste the torment" becomes a formulaic device for closing deniability at the Last Judgment.
- It **reframes language (lisān)** as God's self-imposed constraint (14:4) and humans' self-imposed evasion (41:44).
- It **models disbelief as sensory privation** via the triad ṣumm-bukm-ʿumy (2:18, 2:171, 17:97), carefully expanded in Q 7:179 to show that the organs are present and functional, and that the privation is volitional / cognitive.

The entire sensory system thus maps onto a **two-axis theology**:

- Vertical (God ↔ human): distance senses (hear, see).
- Horizontal (human ↔ world): contact senses (taste, touch, + smell by absence).

The vertical axis is for revelation and judgment, the horizontal for embodiment and retribution. The Quran's theological consistency on this point is enforced not by explicit philosophical argument but by its sheer lexical distribution — a regularity the morphology corpus lets us measure for the first time.

## Hypotheses forwarded to Phase C

- **H-SEN-1.** Divine attributes are lexically restricted to distance senses plus cognitive abstractions; contact senses are grammatically disabled for divine predication. Testable by exhaustive divine-Name corpus survey.
- **H-SEN-2.** The pair samīʿ-baṣīr is prosodically ordered, not theologically ordered: baṣīr finalises because of rhyme. Testable by measuring fāṣila coda distribution across the whole corpus.
- **H-SEN-3.** Dhawq is a judicial device, not a sensory one. Causative `adhāqa` correlates with God-subject; form I `dhāqa` correlates with damned-subject. Testable by agent-patient tagging across the 63 tokens.
- **H-SEN-4.** The ṣumm-bukm-ʿumy triad is a surah-2 signature that migrates into eschatology at 17:97. The triad's order changes at the migration point. Testable by positional metric across all five triad-bearing verses.
- **H-SEN-5.** Q 7:179 is the theoretical cross-reference for 2:18 / 2:171 / 17:97. A ring-compositional analysis should find the four passages organised as an inclusio around the heart-organ doctrine. Testable by deep-pattern ring-centre detection.
